title: Living light: how fireflies and other living things make their own light

summary.text: A firefly makes their own light with chemistry inside their body, to find a partner in the dark. Light made by a living thing is called bioluminescence. Some mushrooms in Meghalaya and the Western Ghats glow too. In the deep sea, where sunlight never reaches, most animals can make light. Living light makes almost no heat.
summary.art: A night scene split in three: fireflies blinking over a paddy field, green mushrooms glowing on a fallen bamboo, and a deep-sea anglerfish with a tiny lamp on their head.

intro.hook: Switch off every light in the room tonight. Wait a little. Now snap a glow stick. It shines, but it has no battery, no wire and no flame. Where is its light coming from?
intro.text: On summer nights before the monsoon, the trees near Bhandardara in Maharashtra begin to sparkle. Thousands of tiny lights blink on and off. They are not lamps. They are fireflies, small beetles that make light inside their own bodies. Far away, deep in the sea, an anglerfish hangs a glowing lure in front of their mouth, in total darkness. How can a living thing make light? And what does the light do for them?
intro.art: A dark tree full of hundreds of tiny yellow-green dots of light, with a child's hand holding a glowing stick in the foreground.

outcomes: I can say what living light is: light that a living thing makes themself, using chemistry inside their body.
I can name living things that glow, like fireflies, glowing mushrooms, deep-sea fish, jellyfish and sea sparkle, and say where they live.
I can explain that a firefly mixes a chemical called luciferin with oxygen to make light, and that this light is cold.
I can give four reasons living things glow: to talk, to catch food, to hide and to scare off an attacker.
I can run a fair test with glow sticks to find out how warmth changes a glow, and say what I think, what I saw and why.
I can tell made light from stored light: a firefly makes their light, but a glow-in-the-dark star only gives back light it soaked up.
I can say what scientists agree on, what they still argue about, and how bright lights at night harm fireflies.

terms.meaning: Something that makes its own light.
terms.example: The Sun, a candle flame, a bulb and a firefly are all light sources.
terms.art: A row of four pictures: the Sun, a diya flame, a bulb and a firefly.

terms.meaning: Light made by a living thing, using chemistry inside their body. Scientists call it bioluminescence. Say it like this: bye-oh-loo-mi-NESS-ence.
terms.example: A firefly's flash is living light.
terms.art: A firefly with their glowing tail end, and the word broken into syllables underneath.

terms.meaning: When two or more substances meet and change into new substances. Some reactions give out heat, and some give out light.
terms.example: Burning a matchstick is a chemical reaction. So is the glow inside a glow stick.
terms.art: A glow stick being bent, with two liquids meeting inside and starting to glow.

terms.meaning: The chemical that reacts with oxygen to give out light inside a glowing living thing. Its name comes from a Latin word meaning light-bringer. Say it like this: loo-SIF-er-in.
terms.example: Inside a firefly's tail, luciferin meets oxygen and gives out light.
terms.art: A tiny glowing drop labelled with a light-bulb symbol, inside a firefly's tail.

terms.meaning: A helper chemical made by the glowing living thing. It makes luciferin and oxygen react quickly. Say it like this: loo-SIF-er-ase.
terms.example: A firefly makes luciferase in their tail, so their flash comes on fast.
terms.art: A pair of tiny hands bringing a luciferin drop and an oxygen bubble together.

terms.meaning: A gas in the air. We breathe it in. Living light needs it too.
terms.example: A firefly switches on their light by letting oxygen reach their lantern.
terms.art: Air bubbles flowing through tiny tubes into a firefly's tail.

terms.meaning: What makes things happen: moving, warming, growing, shining. Energy is never lost. It only changes from one kind to another.
terms.example: A firefly's food gives them energy. Some of that energy comes out as light.
terms.art: A leaf, a firefly eating, then an arrow to a flash of light.

terms.meaning: Light that comes with almost no heat.
terms.example: A glow stick and a firefly both shine but stay cool. An old bulb with a wire inside gets hot.
terms.art: A child's hand happily holding a glow stick, next to a hand pulling away from a hot old-style bulb.

terms.meaning: A small beetle that makes light in the end of their body. In Tamil they are called minmini poochi, and in Hindi jugnu. Fireflies are not really flies.
terms.example: On summer nights, fireflies blink over fields and trees.
terms.art: A close-up beetle with hard wing cases, and a glowing tail end.

terms.meaning: The young form of a firefly, or a wingless female firefly. Many glow-worms glow steadily.
terms.example: Firefly young live in damp soil and leaf litter, and they glow too.
terms.art: A small soft larva glowing on a wet leaf.

terms.meaning: A living thing that is not a plant or an animal. Mushrooms are part of a fungus. Most of the fungus is a web of thin threads hidden in soil or wood.
terms.example: The mushrooms on a rotting log, and the threads inside the log, are one fungus.
terms.art: A cut log showing white threads inside, with mushrooms growing out of the top.

terms.meaning: A mushroom, or a fungus on rotting wood, that makes their own soft green light all night.
terms.example: A glowing mushroom was found on dead bamboo in Meghalaya in 2018.
terms.art: Tiny mushrooms with glowing green stems on a fallen piece of bamboo.

terms.meaning: The part of the ocean far below the surface. Below about 1,000 metres, no sunlight reaches at all. It is dark all day and all night.
terms.example: Anglerfish and many jellyfish live in the deep sea.
terms.art: A tall cut-away of the ocean: bright blue at the top, darker and darker, black at the bottom with tiny glowing animals.

terms.meaning: Something that tempts an animal to come close, so they can be caught.
terms.example: An anglerfish has a glowing lure on a stalk on their head. Small fish swim up to it.
terms.art: An anglerfish with a glowing ball dangling in front of their mouth and a little fish approaching.

terms.meaning: Lights on the underside of a sea animal. They match the faint light from above, so the animal's shadow-shape disappears.
terms.example: A hatchetfish glows on their belly, so hunters below cannot see their dark outline.
terms.art: A small silver fish seen from below, with a row of tiny lights along their belly.

terms.meaning: Very tiny living things, each made of just one cell. Some kinds glow.
terms.example: The lamp on an anglerfish's head is full of glowing bacteria.
terms.art: A magnified view of many tiny rod-shaped bacteria glowing.

terms.meaning: Tiny living things that drift in the sea. Most are too small to see one by one.
terms.example: Sea sparkle is a kind of plankton that glows when the water moves.
terms.art: A drop of seawater magnified to show tiny drifting creatures.

terms.meaning: A tiny glowing plankton, called Noctiluca by scientists. When waves or feet stir them, they flash blue.
terms.example: On some nights, beaches near Mumbai, Goa and Chennai glow blue at the edge of the waves.
terms.art: Waves breaking on a dark Indian beach, the foam glowing blue, with footprints glowing in the wet sand.

terms.meaning: A plastic tube with two liquids inside. When you bend it, they mix and react, and give out light.
terms.example: Glow sticks shine at wedding processions, with no battery.
terms.art: A bent glow stick with a small crack line in the inner glass tube.

terms.meaning: A material that soaks up light, then gives it back slowly in the dark. It does not make new light of its own. Scientists call it phosphorescence.
terms.example: Glow-in-the-dark stars on a ceiling fade after a while, unless a light charges them again.
terms.art: Glowing stars on a bedroom ceiling, some bright, some fading.

terms.meaning: Awake and busy at night.
terms.example: Fireflies, owls and many moths are nocturnal.
terms.art: An owl, a moth and a firefly under a crescent Moon.

terms.meaning: Too much artificial light at night, where it is not needed.
terms.example: A bright street lamp all night can stop fireflies from seeing each other's flashes.
terms.art: A bright lamp post flooding a field with light, and a few lonely fireflies at the dark edge.

terms.meaning: The tiniest bit of light there can be. Light comes in these tiny packets.
terms.example: Each firefly flash is made of a huge number of photons.
terms.art: A firefly flash zoomed in to show it is made of countless tiny dots of light.

explanations.definition: Living light, or bioluminescence, is light that a living thing makes themself, using a chemical reaction inside their body.
explanations.description: Most things we see do not make light. The Moon, a leaf and your hand only send back light from the Sun or a lamp. Things that make their own light are called light sources, like the Sun, a flame and a bulb. A few living things are light sources too. They make light with chemistry, the way a glow stick does, with no fire, wire or battery.
examples: A firefly makes yellow-green flashes in the end of their body.
Some mushrooms glow green all night on rotting wood.
Many deep-sea fish, squid and jellyfish make blue light.
explanations.art: A dark night with three glowing living things: a firefly, a mushroom and a jellyfish, and a Moon labelled with an arrow from the Sun to show it only sends back sunlight.
explanations.context: This card explains the main idea of the whole unit: what living light is.

explanations.concept: How a firefly makes their light
explanations.definition: A firefly makes light when a chemical called luciferin reacts with oxygen from the air. A helper chemical called luciferase makes the reaction happen fast.
explanations.description: The light comes from a part at the end of the firefly's body, called the lantern. The lantern's cells hold luciferin and luciferase, ready to use. They also use energy from the firefly's food. Tiny air tubes bring oxygen into the lantern. When the firefly lets oxygen reach these cells, light comes out. When they hold the oxygen back, the light stops. This is how a firefly switches their light on and off.
examples: In the 1880s, the French scientist Raphael Dubois made two liquids from a glowing click beetle. Both were dark. When he mixed them, they glowed. He named the two chemicals luciferin and luciferase.
Different groups of glowing living things use different luciferins. A firefly's is different from a jellyfish's.
Scientists still argue about exactly how a firefly lets oxygen in and holds it back so quickly.
explanations.art: A cut-away of a firefly's tail: tiny air tubes bringing oxygen bubbles to glowing cells, with labels drawn as pictures, not words.
explanations.context: This card is about what happens inside a firefly's tail when they flash.

explanations.definition: Cold light is light made with almost no heat. Living light is cold light.
explanations.description: Most lights we know get hot. A candle flame burns your finger. An old bulb with a thin wire inside turns most of its energy into heat, and only a little into light. A firefly's lantern is part of their own body. If their light came with that much heat, the firefly would burn themself. Their reaction sends a large share of the energy out as light, and very little as heat. So a glowing firefly feels no warmer than the air around them.
examples: A glow stick stays cool in your hand, even while it shines.
A candle flame gives light, but you feel its heat from above.
LED bulbs also make light with much less heat than old bulbs.
explanations.art: A firefly sitting on a child's open palm, glowing, next to a candle with wavy heat lines above it.
explanations.context: This card explains why a firefly's light does not burn them.

explanations.definition: Fireflies use flashes as signals, to find a partner of their own kind.
explanations.description: A firefly has a problem: they must find a partner of their own kind, at night. There are about 2,000 kinds of fireflies in the world, and several kinds can live in one field. In the dark, a firefly cannot see who is who. So each kind has its own flash code. In many kinds, a male flies about, flashing his pattern. A female waits on a leaf. If the code is her own kind's, she answers after a set wait. He flies down to her. Some fireflies in Asia and America flash all together, so a whole tree blinks on and off at once.
examples: In one American firefly, the male flashes once every few seconds. The female answers about two seconds later.
In the mangroves of Malaysia and Thailand, whole trees of fireflies flash together.
In 1965, an American scientist, James Lloyd, found a trick. Some female fireflies copy the answer of another kind. When a male of that kind flies down, she eats him!
explanations.art: A dark meadow with a flying firefly leaving a dotted trail of flashes, and a firefly on a grass blade answering with one flash.
explanations.context: This card is about why fireflies flash and how they use their light.

explanations.description: All firefly young glow, even before they have wings or a partner to find. So why did glowing begin? Scientists have more than one answer.
examples: Firefly young taste bad to many hunters. A glow may say: do not eat me.
Some baby fireflies glow when touched, like a sudden warning.

perspectives.who: Many firefly scientists, after studying firefly family trees
perspectives.explanation: Glowing began as a warning. Firefly young carry bitter chemicals. Their glow tells toads, mice and birds: I taste terrible. Much later, adult fireflies began to use the same light to talk.
The light chemistry may first have helped fireflies deal with oxygen inside their bodies, which can harm cells. The glow came along by chance, and was only used for signals later.
The warning idea has the most evidence so far. But nobody was there to watch, and the full story is not known.

explanations.art: A small glowing larva on a leaf, and a toad turning their face away.
explanations.context: Scientists agree that fireflies flash to find partners. This card is about why fireflies first began to glow, which is still argued about.

explanations.definition: Glowing mushrooms are fungi that make their own soft green light, using luciferin and oxygen, all through the night.
explanations.description: More than 100 kinds of fungi glow. Often it is not just the mushroom but the thin threads of the fungus inside rotting wood. People long ago called glowing wood foxfire. A fungus does not flash like a firefly. They glow steadily, like a night-light, for as long as they are alive and damp. In 2018, scientists found a new glowing mushroom on dead bamboo near Mawlynnong in Meghalaya. Their stem glows. People there had known about them for a long time.
examples: More than 2,300 years ago, the Greek thinker Aristotle wrote that some rotting wood shines in the dark.
In 1775, an American submarine called the Turtle used glowing foxfire to light the dials inside, so no flame was needed under water.
Glowing mushrooms have also been photographed in the forests of Goa and Kerala, in the monsoon.
explanations.art: Small brown mushrooms on a piece of fallen bamboo, their stems glowing soft green in a dark, damp forest.
explanations.context: This card is about mushrooms and rotting wood that glow in the forest at night.

explanations.description: A firefly flashes to find a partner. But a mushroom has no eyes and no partner to call. So why do they glow?
examples: In a Brazilian forest, scientists put fake glowing mushrooms next to fake dark ones. More insects landed on the glowing ones.
Some glowing fungi glow brightest at night and dimmer in the day. Their glow follows a daily clock.

perspectives.who: Anderson Oliveira, Cassius Stevani and others, studying a Brazilian mushroom in 2015
perspectives.explanation: The glow brings insects. The insects walk over the mushroom and carry away their spores, the tiny specks that grow into new fungi. So the light helps the fungus spread.
For many fungi, the glow may be a side effect. It might be left over from the way they break down wood, or deal with oxygen. The light may have no job at all.
Both may be true for different fungi. Each kind may glow for their own reason.

explanations.art: A glowing mushroom at night with a small beetle and a fly landing on the mushroom.
explanations.context: We know how mushrooms make light. This card is about why they do it, which scientists still argue about.

explanations.concept: The deep sea: the biggest home of living light
explanations.definition: In the deep sea, most animals can make their own light.
explanations.description: Sunlight only goes down a few hundred metres into the sea. Below about 1,000 metres, it is completely dark. There is no day and no night there. Yet many animals live there. In 2017, scientists counted animals filmed by underwater robots in the sea off California. About three out of every four could make light. In the deep sea, almost all the light there is comes from living things.
examples: A lanternfish has rows of tiny lights along their body, like buttons.
Some deep-sea shrimp spit out a cloud of glowing liquid.
Many jellyfish glow when something bumps them.
explanations.art: A deep, black sea dotted with small glowing animals: a lanternfish, a jellyfish, a shrimp and a squid, with a little submarine light far above.
explanations.context: This card is about the deep sea, the part of the ocean that sunlight never reaches.

explanations.concept: Four jobs for light in the dark sea
explanations.definition: Deep-sea animals use light for four main jobs: to catch food, to hide, to scare off attackers, and to talk.
explanations.description: Deep in the sea it is always dark, food is hard to find, and hunters are everywhere. Light helps with each of these problems. Catch: an anglerfish cannot chase food in the dark. They hang a glowing lure in front of their mouth, and small fish swim up to it and are swallowed. Hide: hunters below look up for dark shapes against the faint light from above. A hatchetfish's belly lights match that light, so their shape vanishes. Scare: some jellyfish flash in circles when grabbed. The flashes may call a bigger hunter to eat the attacker. Talk: in the dark, an animal must find their own kind. Some fish and squid have light patterns that only their own kind uses.
examples: The Atolla jellyfish spins a ring of blue flashes when they are caught. Scientists call it a burglar alarm.
The vampire squid squirts glowing slime and swims off in the dark.
In 2012, the scientist Edith Widder built a fake glowing jellyfish called the e-jelly. Its flashes helped film a live giant squid in their deep-sea home, near Japan, for the first time.
explanations.art: Four small panels: an anglerfish with their lure, a hatchetfish with belly lights seen from below, a jellyfish flashing a ring of lights, and two squid flashing at each other.
explanations.context: This card is about why deep-sea animals glow. There are four main reasons.

explanations.definition: Some animals do not make their own light. They keep glowing bacteria inside a special pocket in their bodies.
explanations.description: Some bacteria can glow. But one glowing bacterium is far too faint to see. So these bacteria only switch on their light when there are lots of them together. They tell each other they are there by giving off tiny amounts of a chemical. When enough of the chemical builds up, they all glow at once. An anglerfish's lure is a pocket full of such bacteria. The fish gives them a home and food. The bacteria give the fish their lamp.
examples: The Hawaiian bobtail squid keeps glowing bacteria in a pocket under their body. Their light hides their shadow on moonlit nights. The scientist Margaret McFall-Ngai has studied this squid and their bacteria for many years.
Bonnie Bassler, an American scientist, studies how bacteria count each other with chemicals.
Old fish in a market sometimes glow faintly in the dark, because of glowing bacteria.
explanations.art: A small round squid seen from below, with a glowing patch in their middle, and a zoom circle showing tiny glowing bacteria inside.
explanations.context: This card is about animals that borrow their light from tiny glowing bacteria.

explanations.definition: Sea sparkle is a tiny glowing plankton. They flash blue when the water around them is stirred.
explanations.description: Each sea sparkle is a single cell, just big enough to see as a dot. Small sea animals try to eat them. When something stirs the water around them, they flash blue. Scientists think the sudden flash startles the animals that try to eat them. On most nights there are too few to notice. But sometimes they grow in huge numbers near the coast. Then every breaking wave glows blue, and footprints in wet sand sparkle. Huge numbers of sea sparkle can be a sign that the sea is changing, for example from too much sewage and farm waste washing in.
examples: Beaches near Mumbai, Goa, Mangaluru, Kerala and Chennai have glowed blue on some nights.
On the islands of Lakshadweep and the Andamans, swimmers have seen their arms glow in the water.
Sea sparkle flashes only when disturbed, so the brightest glow is where waves crash.
explanations.art: Night waves breaking on an Indian beach with coconut palms behind, the foam glowing blue and a child's footprints sparkling.
explanations.context: This card is about the blue glow sometimes seen in waves on Indian beaches.

explanations.description: Fireflies, mushrooms, jellyfish, fish and bacteria are not close relatives, and they use different kinds of luciferin. So scientists think living light began separately, again and again. In 2021, two scientists, Emily Lau and Todd Oakley, counted at least 94 separate starts. One study in 2024 suggested that soft corals may have glowed more than 500 million years ago. These are careful best guesses, made by comparing family trees of living things. They may change as we learn more.
examples: Fireflies and click beetles are cousins, and both glow. Even so, a study in 2018 found that they probably began glowing separately.
A glowing mushroom and a glowing fish use completely different chemicals.
No glowing flowering plant has ever been found in nature.
explanations.art: A big branching tree of life with little glowing dots appearing on many separate branches: insects, fungi, fish, jellyfish, bacteria.
explanations.context: This card is about how often living light has appeared in the history of life. It is a best guess, not a certain fact.

explanations.concept: Down to the atoms: chemistry becomes light
explanations.definition: When luciferin reacts with oxygen, a new molecule is made with extra energy. It lets that energy go as a tiny packet of light, a photon.
explanations.description: Everything is made of atoms. Atoms join into groups called molecules. Luciferin is a molecule. When it meets oxygen, its atoms rearrange. For a moment, the new molecule holds extra energy. Scientists say it is 'excited'. It settles down by giving out a photon, the tiniest bit of light. A firefly flash is made of a huge number of photons. So energy from a firefly's food comes out as the energy of light. Energy is never made or destroyed. It only changes form.
examples: A glow stick works the same way, with different molecules.
Fireworks also make light when atoms get extra energy and let it go, but with fire and great heat.
The energy in a firefly's food first came from sunlight, caught by plants.
explanations.art: A zoom from a firefly's tail into a glowing molecule shaped like a ball-and-stick toy, sending out a single bright dot.
explanations.context: This card goes down to atoms, to show how a chemical reaction can make light.

explanations.concept: Living light helps doctors and scientists
explanations.definition: Scientists use the chemicals of living light as tools, to see what is happening inside cells.
explanations.description: In 1961, a Japanese scientist, Osamu Shimomura, studied a glowing jellyfish. He collected thousands of them by hand. From them he found a glowing protein, and another that glows green under blue light. That green protein is now used in labs all over the world. Scientists attach it to parts of a cell, and those parts light up. Shimomura shared a Nobel Prize for this in 2008. Firefly chemicals are also used in hospitals, to check if a surface still has germs on it.
examples: The green jellyfish protein lets scientists watch nerve cells grow in a living worm.
A swab test with firefly chemicals glows if living cells, like germs, are left on a kitchen counter.
In 2020, scientists put genes from a glowing mushroom into a tobacco plant. The plant glowed faintly all their life.
explanations.art: A scientist looking through a microscope at a cell with parts glowing green, with a jar of jellyfish on the bench.
explanations.context: This card is about how people use the chemicals of living light.

explanations.description: Your body makes a very, very faint light. It is about a thousand times too weak for our eyes to see. In 2009, Japanese scientists used a super-sensitive camera in total darkness. They found that faces glowed least in the morning and most in the late afternoon. This light comes from tiny chemical reactions with oxygen in our skin. It is real, but it is not used for anything, as far as we know. Scientists are still finding out what it can tell us.
examples: Most living things give out this ultra-weak light.
Nobody can see it. Only special cameras can catch it.
explanations.art: A dim outline of a child's face in deep darkness, faintly speckled with tiny dots, beside a large camera.
explanations.context: This card is about a surprising finding: people give out a faint light too.

agreed.text: Many living things make their own light, using a chemical reaction. The light comes when a luciferin reacts with oxygen.
agreed.evidence: In the 1880s, Raphael Dubois made a glowing beetle's light in a test tube by mixing two juices from them. Scientists have since found the luciferin chemicals of fireflies, jellyfish, mushrooms and bacteria.

agreed.text: Living light is cold light. It makes almost no heat.
agreed.evidence: A glowing glow stick pressed on your wrist feels no warmer than a whole one. Measurements show that a large share of the reaction's energy leaves as light, not heat.

agreed.text: Fireflies flash to find partners of their own kind.
agreed.evidence: Scientists flash small lights at fireflies in fields. When the light copies a female's answer, males fly down to it.

agreed.text: In the deep sea, most animals can make light.
agreed.evidence: Underwater robots have filmed hundreds of thousands of deep-sea animals. In one count off California, about three in four could glow.

agreed.text: Bright lights at night harm fireflies.
agreed.evidence: In experiments, fireflies near bright lights flash less and find fewer partners. In 2020, firefly experts around the world named light pollution as one of the biggest threats to fireflies, after the loss of their homes.

challenging.claim: Only the Sun, fire and electric lamps can make light.
challenging.who: A common way of thinking, especially in cities where few people see fireflies.
challenging.for: Nearly all the light we use every day comes from the Sun, flames or bulbs.
challenging.against: Fireflies, mushrooms, jellyfish, fish and even bacteria make their own light with chemistry. In the deep sea, living light is the main kind of light there is.
challenging.context: This card looks at a common idea about where light comes from.

challenging.claim: Glowing rotten wood and glowing seas are caused by spirits or by stored sunlight.
challenging.who: Many people in many lands, for thousands of years. Some scientists in the 1600s thought the glow was a kind of slow fire, or stored light.
challenging.for: The glow appears in damp, dark places with no flame and no Sun. It is mysterious.
challenging.against: The glow comes from living fungi and plankton, using luciferin and oxygen. Take away the oxygen, or kill the fungus, and the glow stops.
challenging.context: This card is about old ideas for why rotting wood and seawater sometimes glow.

challenging.claim: Mushrooms glow to bring insects, which spread their spores.
challenging.who: Anderson Oliveira, Cassius Stevani and others, after tests with a Brazilian mushroom in 2015.
challenging.for: More insects landed on fake mushrooms with green lights than on dark ones.
challenging.against: This was tested on one kind. Many other glowing fungi glow inside wood, where spores are not made. For them, the glow may be a side effect.
challenging.context: This card is about an idea for why mushrooms glow, which scientists still argue about.

challenging.who: Many people who remember more fireflies in their childhood, and some news reports.
challenging.for: Fireflies lose their homes when wetlands and fields are built over. Bright lights and pesticides harm them too. Many grandparents say they saw more.
challenging.against: For most places, including India, there are very few long, careful counts. Some kinds are surely in trouble. For others, we do not know.
challenging.context: This card is about whether fireflies really are disappearing.

challenging.claim: Living light is a rare oddity in nature.
challenging.who: Scientists long ago, who studied mostly animals on land.
challenging.for: On land, only a few animals glow, like fireflies and some worms.
challenging.against: Scientists now think living light began separately at least 94 times. In the open sea and deep sea, most animals can glow. Some scientists, such as Edith Widder, think light may be the most common way animals signal to each other on Earth.
challenging.context: This card is about whether living light is rare or common.

big_questions.q: A firefly eats food, and later makes light. How can food turn into light?
big_questions.hint: Food holds energy. Where did the energy in the food come from first?

big_questions.q: Why does a firefly's light not burn them?
big_questions.hint: Think of the glow stick you held.

big_questions.q: If all the fireflies in a field flashed at exactly the same moment, how would they know when to flash?
big_questions.hint: Each firefly can see their neighbours. What would you do in a clapping game?

big_questions.q: Why do so many deep-sea animals glow, but so few animals on land?
big_questions.hint: On land, what lights up the day? What is there in the deep sea?

big_questions.q: A mushroom has no eyes. Why would they make light?
big_questions.hint: Who else might see the light? What might they do?

big_questions.q: The glowing mushrooms of Meghalaya were known to local people long before scientists named them. Who really discovered them?
big_questions.hint: What is the difference between knowing something and writing it down for the world?

big_questions.q: We light up our cities at night. Who else lives in the night, and what do they need?
big_questions.hint: Think of fireflies, owls, moths and turtles.

big_questions.q: A trickster firefly copies another kind's answer flash to catch males. How could a male tell a real partner from a trickster?
big_questions.hint: Think about the wait before the answer, and what else the male could watch for as he flies closer.

big_questions.q: Your body gives out a faint light that nobody can see. What else might be real but too faint for us to notice?
big_questions.hint: Think of sounds too high to hear, or smells only dogs notice.

big_questions.q: In the daytime, the glowing mushrooms look plain and brown. What does that tell us about seeing things only in one kind of light?
big_questions.hint: Think of the stars in the daytime sky. Are they still there at noon?

story.title: The Lamps That Stay
story.note: Glowing bamboo mushrooms really grow near Mawlynnong in Meghalaya. Scientists found them in 2018, and people there had long known them. Iba, Phrang, their grandmother and this night are made up.
text: The rain stopped just as the sun went down, and the whole forest dripped. Iba was eleven. Her brother Phrang was six. They had spent the afternoon at their aunt's house in the next village, eating red rice and smoky dal, and listening to their cousins argue. Now they were walking home along the bamboo path, the way they had walked a hundred times in daylight.
"Stay by the stream," their mother had said that morning. "The stream knows the way home, even when you don't."
Iba carried the torch. It was an old one, with a crack in the glass. Its beam was already yellow and tired. Halfway home, under the tallest bamboo, it flickered twice and went out.

The dark came down all at once. It was not like the dark of their room at night, with a little grey at the window. Clouds covered the sky. There was no Moon and not a single star. Iba held up her hand in front of her face. She could not see it at all.
Phrang found her sleeve and held on with both fists. "Iba," he whispered. "I can't see anything."
"Neither can I," said Iba, because she did not believe in lying to him, even now.
They stood still. The stream chattered somewhere to their left. Water dripped from leaves. A frog said one word and stopped.

Then, ahead of them, a tiny light blinked on. It blinked off. Another blinked on, higher up, and then another, low among the ferns. Soon there were dozens, golden-green, flashing and gone, flashing and gone.
"Jugnu!" said Phrang. He was not whispering any more. "Iba, look! They came to show us the way!"
He let go of her sleeve and ran towards them.

"Phrang, wait!" Iba ran after him. She caught his shirt and held it. They had left the path. She could feel it. The ground under her feet was soft and full of roots. The fireflies were all around them now, flashing everywhere and nowhere. When Iba stepped towards one, they went dark, and another lit up behind her. She turned, and turned again. She could no longer hear the stream.
Her heart was banging. She made herself breathe slowly, the way her grandmother breathed before she began a long story.

Her grandmother liked fireflies. She said they were the most talkative creatures in the hills. "All night they say, here I am, here I am, where are you?" she would say. "But they are not talking to us, child. They are talking to each other. A firefly goes wherever they like."

Iba looked at the flashing lights again. They were not leading anywhere. They were calling to each other, in a language that had nothing to do with two children lost in a wet forest. Following them was like following someone else's conversation.
"They're not for us," she said quietly. "Phrang, sit down with me for a moment. Close your eyes and count to twenty. Then open them, and look low. Look at the ground, not the air."

Phrang counted, very fast. Iba counted slowly. When she opened her eyes, the forest was just as black. But now she saw something she had missed. Down near the ground, a little way off, there was a faint smudge of green. It did not blink. It did not move. It just glowed, soft as a breath on cold glass.

She crept towards it on her hands and knees, with Phrang holding her ankle. It was a fallen bamboo, old and rotting, half sunk in wet leaves. Along its side grew tiny mushrooms, no bigger than her fingernail. Their thin stems were shining green. She held her hand close. She felt no warmth at all. The light was cool, like water.
"Who lit them?" whispered Phrang.
"Nobody," said Iba. "There's no Moon to shine on them. There's no torch. They're making the light themselves." Saying it out loud made the hairs on her arms stand up.

And then she understood something else. Bamboo grows thickest by water. When old bamboo falls, it falls near where it grew. And the glowing mushrooms grow only on fallen bamboo that is old and damp. They do not fly about. They stay where they are, all night long.
She looked past the first glow. There, a few steps further on, was another faint green smudge. And past that, another, and another, like a dotted line drawn in the dark.
"Hold my hand," she said. "We'll walk from one green light to the next. Only the ones that stay still."

They went slowly. The fireflies flashed all around their heads, busy with their own lives. Iba ignored them. She kept her eyes low, on the steady glows. At the fourth one, she heard it: the stream, chattering on her left again. At the seventh, her feet found the hard, smooth path.
Far ahead, a lantern was swinging. It was their mother, calling their names.

Phrang ran to her. Iba stopped and looked back once. Behind her, the line of small green lamps lay along the stream, quiet and patient. The fireflies were still flashing above them, still saying here I am, where are you, to someone who was not her.

The next morning, she walked back alone in the sunshine to find the mushrooms. She found the bamboo easily. The mushrooms were still there. But in daylight they were just tiny brown things, so plain that nobody would look twice. Their light had not gone anywhere. It was only that the Sun was so much brighter.
Iba crouched beside them for a long time. Then she said thank you, softly, which felt silly and right at the same time.
story.epiphany: For the parent: there are two kinds of living light in this story, and they do different jobs. The fireflies flash to talk to each other. Their lights move, switch on and off, and lead nowhere for a human. The mushrooms glow steadily all night, and they stay where they grow, on old bamboo by the stream. Iba gets home by telling the two apart. She also realises the light cannot be borrowed, because there is no Moon or torch. The mushrooms make it themselves, and it is cold. In the morning she sees their light was there all along, just hidden by brighter sunlight.
ask: Why did Iba stop following the fireflies? What were the fireflies really doing with their flashes?
How was the mushrooms' light different from the fireflies' light?
How did Iba know the mushrooms were making their own light, and not just shining back the light of something else?
Why did the line of glowing mushrooms lead back to the stream?
In the morning the mushrooms looked plain and brown. Where had their light gone? Can you think of other things we only notice in the dark?

games.title: Flash and Answer: the firefly torch game
games.players: 2 to 4 players, in a dark room or outside after sunset; a grown-up helps
games.context: This is a game where you pretend to be fireflies. Fireflies are beetles that flash light to find a partner of their own kind. Each player gets a secret code card and a torch.

printables.title: 10 secret firefly cards to cut out
items: Jugnu kind A. Your flash: 1 long. Your answer: wait 2 seconds, then 1 short.
Jugnu kind A. Your flash: 1 long. Your answer: wait 2 seconds, then 1 short.
Jugnu kind B. Your flash: 2 short. Your answer: wait 1 second, then 2 short.
Jugnu kind B. Your flash: 2 short. Your answer: wait 1 second, then 2 short.
Jugnu kind C. Your flash: 3 short, fast. Your answer: wait 3 seconds, then 1 long.
Jugnu kind C. Your flash: 3 short, fast. Your answer: wait 3 seconds, then 1 long.
Jugnu kind D. Your flash: 1 short and 1 long. Your answer: wait 2 seconds, then 1 long.
Jugnu kind D. Your flash: 1 short and 1 long. Your answer: wait 2 seconds, then 1 long.
TRICKSTER (copies kind A). You have no flash of your own. When a kind A firefly flashes, answer like kind A: wait 2 seconds, then 1 short. If the flyer walks to you, you take the token.
TRICKSTER (copies kind B). You have no flash of your own. When a kind B firefly flashes, answer like kind B: wait 1 second, then 2 short. If the flyer walks to you, you take the token.

printables.title: 2 event cards to cut out
items: STREET LAMP. During the first flyer's turn this round, one player holds a bright torch still, pointing at the wall. Nobody can see the flashes, so nobody answers and nobody takes a token.
SYNC TREE. Everyone flashes together on the count of three, five times, like the fireflies that blink together in a tree. Then everyone takes one token.

printables.title: Partner tokens: cut 20 small paper circles
items: Cut 20 small paper circles. Each is one partner token.

rules: Choose the firefly cards for your group. With 2 players, use kind A, kind B and both TRICKSTER cards (6 cards). With 3 players, add kind C (8 cards). With 4 players, use all 10. Keep the 2 event cards in a separate face-down pile. Put the tokens in the middle.
Play 2 rounds. At the start of a round, shuffle the firefly cards and deal one to each player, face down. Look at your own card only. Then turn over the top event card and do what it says.

Each player holding a kind card is the flyer once, one after another. A player holding a TRICKSTER card is a waiter all round and has no flyer turn. The flyer flashes the code on their card with a torch pointed at the floor, up to 3 times, never at anyone's eyes. Everyone else sits still as a waiter.
A waiter holding the same kind answers after the wait on their card. A waiter holding a TRICKSTER answers like the kind on their card, if the flyer is that kind. Everyone else stays quiet.

If someone answers, the flyer walks to them and both show their cards. If the kinds match, each takes a token. If it is a TRICKSTER, only the trickster takes a token. If two players answer, the flyer chooses one.
If nobody answers, nobody takes a token. After every flyer has had a turn, the round ends.
After 2 rounds, the player with the most tokens wins. If it is a tie, everyone wins.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the cards. 2. Choose the cards for your group, as in rule 1. 3. Give each player a torch. 4. Darken the room, but leave a dim light in the corridor.
flow.say: Fireflies are beetles that make light in their tails. Each kind has its own flash code. Tonight, we are fireflies. You will find a partner using only flashes.
flow.kid: Take a torch. Later you will get a secret card. Don't show anyone! Point your torch at the floor. Never shine it in someone's eyes.
flow.context: This is the first step of Flash and Answer, a firefly game played with torches in the dark. Here you set up the game.
flow.parent: Small torches or phone torches work. Keep the room dim, not pitch dark, so nobody trips.

flow.do: Play one practice round together. Both of you hold a kind A card. You flash kind A's code. Your child, as a waiter, answers.
flow.say: Watch my flash. One long. Now wait two seconds, and answer with one short flash. Good! That's how fireflies say, I'm here, are you my kind?
flow.kid: Watch the flash. One long. Count two seconds. Now flash one short back. You found a partner!

check.q: A firefly flashes a code, and another firefly flashes back. What is the answer flash for?
options: To say: I am your kind, come here
To light up the path so they can see
To scare away hunters
To keep warm
check.why: Fireflies flash to find a partner of their own kind. The answer says: I am here, and I am your kind. Picking 'light up the path' usually means thinking fireflies use light like a torch. Their flashes are messages, not lamps. Picking 'keep warm' misses that firefly light is cold light.

flow.do: Play the game for 2 rounds, as in the rules. Remember the event card at the start of each round.
flow.say: Flyers, flash your code. Waiters, watch carefully. Answer only if the code is your own kind.
flow.kid: Look at your secret card. When it is your turn, flash your code at the floor. Watch for an answer. Is it your kind? Walk over and show cards.
flow.parent: Watch what happens when the STREET LAMP card is played: nobody can find anyone. This is like real fireflies near bright lights. The trickster cards are based on real fireflies, described by the scientist James Lloyd in 1965.

ask.q: What happened when the street lamp was on?
good: We couldn't see each other's flashes.
The bright light drowned out the flashes.

flow.do: Switch on the lights. Count the tokens and talk about the game.
flow.say: Who found the most partners? Was anyone tricked? Now think about real fireflies. What would happen to them if every field had a bright lamp all night?
flow.kid: Count your tokens. Were you tricked? Think about real fireflies. What would a bright lamp do to them?

check.q: In the game, a bright street lamp stopped everyone finding partners. Why is this a problem for real fireflies?
options: Bright light at night hides their flashes, so they can't find partners
Fireflies are scared of lamps and fly away for ever
Lamps make fireflies too hot
It is not a problem, fireflies like lamps
check.why: Fireflies talk with faint flashes. A bright light nearby drowns them out, so males and females miss each other. Fewer partners means fewer baby fireflies. Picking 'too hot' usually means thinking all light is hot. Picking 'fireflies like lamps' may come from seeing moths at lamps. Moths and fireflies behave differently.

printables.title: 4 action cards to cut out
items: HUNTER: a hunter swims by. If your HIDE mat is still empty, put one card from your hand on the discard pile.
SWAP: swap one card from your hand with the player on your left.
SUNLIGHT: sunlight! Every glow is hard to see. Your turn ends and you place no card.
CAMERA: a scientist's camera arrives. Name any glowing animal and say what the light is for. If the others agree, draw one more card and play a card as normal.

printables.title: Four job mats: make one set for each player
items: CATCH: light to catch food
HIDE: light to vanish
SCARE: light to frighten or call help
TALK: light to find your own kind

rules: Each player lays out their own four job mats. Shuffle all 18 cards. Deal 3 to each player. Put the rest face down as the pile.
On your turn, draw the top card. If it is an action card, do what it says, then put it on the discard pile. Your turn is over.

If you drew an animal card, you now hold one more card than at the start. Pick one animal card from your hand, read the card aloud, and say how the animal's light helps with that job. Place the card on the matching job mat if that mat is empty.
Not sure which job it is? The other players may help you. If your mat for that job is already full, or you do not want to place a card, put one card from your hand on the discard pile instead.
The first player with a card on all four of their mats wins. If the pile runs out first, finish that round of turns. The player with the most mats filled wins. If it is a tie, everyone wins.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the cards and the four mats. 2. Lay your four mats in a row. 3. Shuffle the 18 cards and deal 3 cards each.
flow.say: Deep in the sea it is completely dark. Most animals there make their own light. Each card is a real animal. Your job is to say why they glow.
flow.kid: Lay out your four mats: catch, hide, scare, talk. Take 3 cards. Each animal card is a real animal.
flow.context: This is the first step of Deep Dark Sea, a card game about why deep-sea animals glow. Here you set up the game.

flow.do: Play the anglerfish card together as a practice.
flow.say: The anglerfish has a glowing ball dangling from their head, right in front of their mouth. Which job is that?
flow.kid: Anglerfish. A glowing ball hangs in front of their mouth. Catch, hide, scare or talk?

check.q: An anglerfish dangles a glowing ball in front of their mouth. What is the light for?
options: To catch food
To see where they are going
To keep warm
To hide
check.why: Small fish swim towards the glowing lure, and the anglerfish snaps them up. Picking 'to see where they are going' usually means thinking of the light as a headlamp. Their light is bait, not a torch. Picking 'keep warm' misses that living light is cold.

flow.do: Take turns, as in the rules. Draw, read an animal card aloud, and place the card on the right mat.
flow.say: Read your card. Which job? And how does the light do that job?
flow.kid: Read your card. Put it on a mat. Say how their light helps.
flow.parent: The tricky job is HIDE. It seems strange to hide by glowing. Explain it like this: from below, a fish looks like a dark shape against the faint light above. Belly lights fill in the dark shape, so it disappears. The Atolla jellyfish card is a burglar alarm: their flashes may call a bigger hunter to eat the attacker.

check.q: A hatchetfish glows on their belly. How can light help them hide?
options: The glow matches the faint light from above, so their dark shape vanishes
The glow blinds every hunter for ever
The glow makes the fish look much bigger
Glowing can never help you hide
check.why: From below, any fish shows up as a dark outline against the dim light from above. A glowing belly fills in that outline. Picking 'glowing can never help you hide' is a very natural thought, because on land, a light gives you away. In the deep sea, being dark from below is what gives you away.

flow.do: Finish the game. Then spread out all 14 animal cards and sort them by job.
flow.say: Which job do the most animals do? Why do you think so many animals in the dark sea glow?
flow.kid: Sort all the animal cards by job. Count each group. Which job has the most animals?
flow.think: If you lived in the dark deep sea, which glowing job would you choose?
