items.p: Kavya, a girl in Class 3, sees a firefly blink on a dark night. Next morning she sees a green leaf shining in the sunshine. Which one is making their own light?
items.why: The firefly makes new light with chemistry inside their body. That is living light, or bioluminescence. The leaf only sends back sunlight that lands on it. Picking 'both' mixes up making light and sending back light. In a dark room, the leaf would show nothing.
items.art: A firefly glowing at night beside a leaf lit by the morning Sun.

items.p: Sort these. Does each one make their own light, or not?
cats: Does not make their own light
items: a firefly
Makes their own light
the Moon
Does not make their own light
a glowing mushroom
Makes their own light
a mirror
Does not make their own light
the glowing bacteria in an anglerfish's lure
Makes their own light
a white cat in torchlight
Does not make their own light
items.a: see items
items.why: Living light is made by the living being themself. The Moon, a mirror and a cat in torchlight only send back light from somewhere else. A strong answer puts the white cat in 'does not', even though the cat is alive: being alive is not the same as glowing.

items.p: A firefly makes light when a chemical called luciferin meets the gas ____ from the air.
items.why: Oxygen from the air reacts with luciferin, and light comes out. The firefly switches their light on by letting air into their lantern.

items.p: Anything that gives out light must also be hot.
items.why: False, though most people think so, because bulbs and flames are hot. A firefly and a glow stick give out light with almost no heat. This is called cold light.

items.p: Remember the cold light test? You pressed a glowing glow stick and a whole one on your wrist. What did your wrist feel each time? What does this tell you about a firefly's light?
items.a: Both sticks felt the same on my wrist, and neither was warm. So a glow can be cold. A firefly's light is cold light too, so the lantern does not harm their body.
items.why: A strong answer says what was felt each time, then uses it to explain why a firefly's lantern can be part of their body.

items.p: Why do most fireflies flash?
opts: To find a partner of their own kind
To see where they are flying
items.why: Each kind of firefly has their own flash code, and they flash to find a partner. Picking 'to see where they are flying' treats the flash as a torch, but their flashes are messages. Picking 'keep warm' misses that firefly light is cold.

items.p: Match each glowing living being to where they live.
pairs: fields and gardens on warm nights
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Living light is found on land, in forests and all through the sea.

items.p: In the glow stick test, the stick in warm water glowed brightest, and the one in icy water glowed dimmest. Explain why. Use the word 'reaction'.
items.a: The light comes from a chemical reaction inside the stick. Warmth makes the reaction go faster, so more light comes out every second. Cold slows the reaction, so less light comes out.
items.why: A strong answer links brightness to how fast the reaction runs, not to the water giving the stick light or heat to shine with.

items.p: You shine a torch on a glow-in-the-dark star, then switch off the light. The star glows. Is it making its own light, like a firefly?
opts: No, it is giving back light it soaked up from the torch
Yes, it makes light from the air
items.why: The star stores light, then lets it out slowly. A firefly makes new light with a chemical reaction. Picking 'just like a firefly' mixes up glowing and making light. A star kept in a dark drawer all day does not glow at all.

items.p: Deep in the sea, below about 1,000 metres, how much sunlight is there?
opts: Lots, because water makes light brighter
items.why: Sunlight fades as it goes down through water. Below about 1,000 metres it is completely dark, day and night. Picking 'a little at midday' is right for a few hundred metres down, but not for the deep sea.

items.p: Most animals in the deep sea can make their own light.
items.why: True. In one count of deep-sea animals off California, about three out of every four could glow. In the dark, light is the best way to signal, trick or hide.

items.p: An anglerfish has a glowing ball dangling in front of their mouth. What is it for?
opts: To bring small fish close, so the anglerfish can eat them
items.why: The glowing lure is bait. Small fish swim up to the light and are swallowed. Picking 'to see in the dark' treats the lure as a headlamp. Picking 'to hide' mixes it up with belly lights.

items.p: Draw a firefly at night. Show where their light comes from. Draw an arrow for the air going in.
items.a: A beetle with their glowing lantern at the end of their body, and an arrow of air going into the lantern.
items.why: The light comes from the lantern, where luciferin meets oxygen from the air. A strong drawing shows the light at the back end, not the head.

items.p: A park in Chennai has fireflies. The town wants to put up bright lights along the path. Three people disagree.

views.who: Meena, who walks home through the park late at night
views.says: The path needs bright lights all night. People must feel safe.
Bright lights hide the fireflies' flashes, so they find fewer partners. Keep the park dark.

views.who: Lakshmi, who looks after the park
views.says: Use dim lights that point down at the path, and switch them off after midnight.

items.ask: Which plan do you choose? Give a reason from what you learned about fireflies. Then say what the person you disagree with has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks a plan and explains it with firefly science: fireflies flash to find partners, and bright light drowns out their flashes. It then gives the other side a fair point, for example that people really do need to see the path. It may mix ideas, like shaded lamps that light only the ground.
items.why: This is a real trade-off. People's safety and the fireflies' dark both matter. Light pollution is one of the biggest dangers to fireflies, along with losing the places they live.

items.p: Name two living beings that make light. Say what each one uses their light for.
items.a: For example: a firefly flashes to find a partner. An anglerfish uses their glowing lure to catch small fish.
items.why: Any two correct living beings, each with a real job for their light, make a strong answer.

items.p: Light made by living beings is called bio____.
items.why: Bioluminescence means living light. 'Bio' means life, and 'luminescence' means giving out light.

items.p: Inside a firefly, a helper chemical called luciferase is part of making light. What does luciferase do?
opts: Makes luciferin and oxygen react quickly
items.why: Luciferase is a helper that speeds up the reaction, so the flash comes on fast. Picking 'stores sunlight' mixes up living light and glow-in-the-dark stars. Picking 'cools the firefly' misses that the light is already cold.

items.p: In the glow stick test, the stick in warm water glowed brightest. Next morning it is the first to be dark. What is the best reason?
opts: It used up its chemicals faster
The warm water put the light out
items.why: Warmth makes the reaction run faster, so the stick shines brighter but spends its chemicals sooner. Picking 'put the light out' mixes up warm and hot. The stick did not stop because of the water; it ran out.

items.p: Some jellyfish flash a ring of lights when they are grabbed. Scientists call this a burglar alarm. Why?
opts: The flashes may call a bigger hunter to eat the attacker
The flashes wake the jellyfish up
items.why: Like an alarm, the flashes draw attention. A bigger animal may come and eat whatever grabbed the jellyfish. Picking 'warm the water' misses that living light is cold.

items.p: Remember the vanishing fish? The paper fish almost disappeared when the torch made them as bright as the screen behind. Why does this help a real hatchetfish hide from a hunter swimming below?
items.a: From below, a fish looks like a dark shape against the faint light coming down from above. The hatchetfish's belly lights fill in that shape, so the shape matches the light behind. Then the hunter cannot see an outline.
items.why: A strong answer says the danger is a dark outline, and that the belly lights hide it by matching the light from above. This trick is called counter-illumination.

items.p: Draw what a hunter looking up from below would see: one hatchetfish with their belly lights on, and one with their belly lights off.
items.a: The fish with lights off is a clear dark shape against the pale water above. The fish with lights on is very faint, nearly the same as the water.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the dark outline is what gives a fish away, and that belly light hides the outline.

items.p: Where does the light in an anglerfish's lure come from?
opts: From glowing bacteria living inside the lure
items.why: Tiny glowing bacteria live in the lure. The fish gives them a home and food, and they give the fish a lamp. Picking 'the Sun' misses that sunlight never reaches the deep sea.

items.p: Glowing bacteria only light up when there are lots of them together.
items.why: True. Each one gives off a chemical to tell the others they are there. When enough builds up, they all glow at once. One alone would make too little light to be useful.

items.p: In the story The Lamps That Stay, Iba got home by following the glowing mushrooms, not the fireflies. Why did that work?
opts: The mushrooms glowed steadily and stayed where they grew, by the stream
The fireflies were too hot to go near
The mushrooms were brighter than the Sun
items.why: Fireflies flash and move about, talking to each other. The mushrooms stay on old bamboo by the stream, glowing all night. Picking 'too hot' misses that firefly light is cold.
items.context: In the story The Lamps That Stay, Iba, a girl of eleven, and her little brother are lost at night in a forest in Meghalaya. Fireflies flash all around them, and glowing mushrooms grow on fallen bamboo.

items.p: Put the steps of a firefly flash in order.
items: The firefly lets air into their lantern
Oxygen meets luciferin
Luciferase makes the reaction fast
Light comes out
The firefly stops the air, and the light goes off
items.why: Air brings oxygen. Oxygen reacts with luciferin, helped by luciferase. Light comes out. Shutting off the air stops the light.

items.p: Sea sparkle, tiny living beings in the sea, glow brightest where waves crash.
items.why: True. Sea sparkle flash when the water around them is stirred. So the brightest glow is in breaking waves and around moving feet.

items.p: Some female fireflies copy the answer flash of a different kind of firefly. What happens when a male of that kind flies down to her?
items.why: The scientist James Lloyd found these trickster fireflies in 1965. They use light as a trap. Picking 'become partners' misses that she is a different kind, and the copied answer is a trap to catch food.

items.p: Match each deep-sea light to the job it does.
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Deep-sea animals use light for four main jobs: to catch food, to hide, to scare attackers and to talk.

items.p: Why do you think so many deep-sea animals make light, but so few animals on land do?
items.a: On land, the Sun lights up the day, so many animals can see without making light. In the deep sea it is dark all the time. Making light is the only way to signal, trick or hide with light down there.
items.why: A strong answer links glowing to the darkness of the deep sea, and compares it with daylight on land.

items.p: In the 1880s, a French scientist, Raphael Dubois, made two juices from the glowing part of a click beetle. Each juice was dark on its own. When he mixed them in a tube, they glowed. What does this tell us about living light?
items.a: Living light comes from chemicals. It can even happen outside the animal's body, if the right chemicals and oxygen are mixed. It is chemistry, not magic.
items.why: A strong answer says the light needs two chemicals together, and that it works outside the body. Dubois named them luciferin and luciferase.

items.p: All baby fireflies glow, long before they need to find a partner. So why did fireflies first start glowing? Scientists give different answers.

views.says: Glowing began as a warning. Baby fireflies taste bitter. Their glow tells toads and birds: do not eat me.
The light chemistry first helped fireflies deal with oxygen inside their bodies. The glow came along by chance and was used for signals later.

items.ask: Which idea do you find more likely? Give a reason. Then say what evidence could change your mind.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side and uses a real clue, for example that baby fireflies glow when touched, like a sudden warning. It then names evidence that would help decide, such as whether hunters really learn to avoid glowing young. It admits nobody was there to watch.
items.why: Scientists still argue about this. The warning idea has the most evidence so far, but the full story is not known.

items.p: A firefly eats food and later makes light. Where did the energy in their food first come from?
items.why: Plants catch sunlight to make food. Animals eat plants, or eat animals that ate plants. So a firefly's flash is sunlight energy, changed many times. Picking 'their own light' goes the wrong way round. Light is where the energy ends up.

items.p: Down at the level of atoms, how does luciferin make light?
opts: The new molecule has extra energy and lets it go as tiny packets of light
It catches sunlight and holds it
items.why: After luciferin reacts with oxygen, the new molecule holds extra energy. It settles down by giving out a photon, the tiniest bit of light. Picking 'catches sunlight' mixes it up with glow-in-the-dark stars. Picking 'catches fire' misses that there is no flame or heat.

items.p: A glowing mushroom and a firefly use exactly the same chemicals to make their light.
items.why: False. Both use a luciferin and oxygen, but the luciferins are different chemicals. Fungi, fireflies, jellyfish and bacteria each found their own way to make light.

items.p: Living light began separately at least 94 times, in very different living beings. What does that suggest about making light in the dark?
items.a: It suggests that making light is very useful in the dark. Again and again, different living beings found their own way to do it, because it helped them find food, hide, warn or find a partner.
items.why: A strong answer links 'many separate beginnings' to 'very useful'. When the same ability appears many times, it usually helps living beings survive.

items.p: In Brazil, scientists put fake glowing mushrooms next to fake dark ones in a forest. More insects landed on the glowing ones. What does this suggest?
opts: The glow may bring insects that spread the mushroom's spores
Insects are scared of the dark
It proves every mushroom glows for this reason
items.why: This test, in 2015, suggests one reason for one kind of mushroom. Picking 'it proves every mushroom' goes too far. One test on one kind cannot tell us about all fungi.

items.p: A friend's grandmother says there were many more fireflies when she was a child. Is that good evidence that fireflies are disappearing? How could you find out for sure?
items.a: It is a useful clue, but memories can be wrong or patchy. To find out for sure, many people would need to count fireflies in the same places, at the same time, every year, and compare the counts.
items.why: A strong answer takes the memory seriously but asks for counts that can be compared. Scientists say there are very few long counts of fireflies in India.

items.p: Here are made-up results from a firefly count, three minutes each night. Night 2 was cool and windy. Give two possible reasons why the count was low that night. How could you check which reason is right?
items.a: Fireflies may flash less when it is cool, because the cold slows the chemistry in their bodies. Or the wind may keep them from flying. To check, count on many nights and write down the warmth and the wind each time. Then see which one goes with low counts.
items.why: A strong answer gives two different reasons, links one of them to the glow stick test, and plans more counts to compare. One low night is not enough to decide.

chart.title: Made-up example: firefly flashes counted in 3 minutes

items.p: Scientists use the chemicals of living light as tools. Match each one to what it is used for.
pairs: A green glowing protein from a jellyfish
makes parts of cells light up under a microscope
glow if germs are left on a kitchen counter
Glowing bacteria in a water sample
dim if the water has poison in it
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Osamu Shimomura found the green protein in a jellyfish and shared a Nobel Prize for it in 2008. Each tool works because living light shows where living cells are, or whether they are healthy.

items.p: Your body gives out a very faint light, about a thousand times too weak for your eyes to see.
items.why: True. In 2009, scientists in Japan photographed it with a super-sensitive camera in total darkness. What it can tell us is still being studied.

items.p: Most deep-sea animals cannot see red light. A black dragonfish shines a red light from under their eyes, and they can see red. How might that help the dragonfish?
opts: They can light up small animals to eat, without being seen
Red light keeps them warm in the cold sea
Red light tells other animals to stay away
items.why: The red light works like a secret torch. The dragonfish sees the small animals in their red light, but those animals cannot see the light, so they do not swim away. Picking 'stay away' would only work if the others could see red. Picking 'keeps them warm' misses that living light is cold.

items.p: Glowing bamboo mushrooms grow near Mawlynnong in Meghalaya. Scientists found them in 2018 and gave them a name a few years later. Who discovered them?

views.who: A woman who has lived in Mawlynnong all her life
views.says: We have known these glowing mushrooms for a long time. We found them first.

views.who: A scientist who helped name them
views.says: We studied them, compared them with other fungi and gave them a name. Now scientists everywhere can find out about them.

items.ask: Who should get the credit? Give a reason. Then say what the other side adds.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side with a reason, for example that people who knew the mushrooms first discovered them. It then says what the other side adds, for example that naming and studying let the whole world learn about them. It may say both should be credited.
items.why: This is a real question about fairness and about different ways of knowing. Local knowledge came first. Science shared it widely. Both matter.

items.p: A cookiecutter shark is a small shark that takes round bites out of bigger fish. Their belly glows all over, except for a dark collar. From below, the collar may look like a small fish. Why might that help the shark?
opts: Bigger fish swim up to catch the 'small fish', and the shark bites them instead
items.why: The dark patch may work as a lure, like the anglerfish's glow. Light and dark can both be used to trick. Picking 'keeps warm' misses that living light is cold.

items.p: Draw a deep-sea scene with three animals. Give each one a light with a different job: catch food, hide, scare an attacker or talk. Label the jobs.
items.a: For example, an anglerfish with a lure (catch food), a hatchetfish with belly lights (hide), and a jellyfish flashing a ring (scare).
items.why: A strong drawing puts each light on the part of the body where real animals have it, and matches it to a job that light really does in the dark sea.

items.p: Why do glowing mushrooms look plain and brown in the daytime?
opts: Their faint glow is still there, but sunlight is far brighter
They stop being alive in the day
items.why: A faint light is hard to see next to a bright one. In the dark, the same faint glow stands out. Picking 'stop being alive' misses that the mushroom lives day and night. Some fungi do glow a little dimmer by day, but mostly the sunlight hides the glow.

items.p: In the glow-in-the-dark star test, star A got 10 seconds of torchlight and glowed for 3 minutes. Star B got 60 seconds and glowed for 7 minutes. Priya, a girl in Class 4, says, 'So the stars make light, like fireflies.' What is wrong with her thinking?
items.a: The results show the opposite. The more light the star soaked up, the longer it glowed. So it is giving back stored light, not making new light. A firefly makes new light from chemicals, even in a dark room.
items.why: A strong answer uses the numbers as evidence: more light in gave more glow out. It contrasts this with a firefly, who needs no light to glow.

experiments.title: Warm Glow, Cold Glow: does warmth change a glow stick?
experiments.context: This is the glow stick test. You put glow sticks in cold, room-temperature and warm water, then compare how bright they glow. A glow stick makes light with a chemical reaction, a bit like a firefly does.
experiments.question: Does a glow stick glow brighter in cold water or in warm water?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Will the glow stick in warm water be brighter, dimmer or the same as the one in cold water? Say why.
experiments.fair_test: To make it fair, change only one thing: how warm the water is. Use three glow sticks of the same colour and size, from the same packet. Snap them at the same moment. Use the same amount of water in the same kind of glass.
results_table: Still glowing next morning? (yes, faint or no)

materials.item: 3 glow sticks of the same colour and size
3 clear glasses, or steel tumblers that you look into from the top
ice cubes and cold water
warm water from a tap or a kettle, cooled until it is comfortable for a hand
a dark room or a bathroom with the light off
space in the fridge for one glass overnight

experiments.safety: A grown-up handles the warm water. It should be warm like a bath, never boiling. Never cut or bite a glow stick. If one leaks, wash hands and do not touch eyes.

schedule.what: Guess. Set up three glasses. Snap the glow sticks and drop them in. Compare the glow in the dark. Put the icy glass in the fridge.
Next morning, take the icy stick out and compare all three in the dark. Say what you think, what you saw and why.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Rank the brightness 1, 2 and 3. Next morning, write whether each one still glows.

setup.art: Three steel tumblers in a row: one with ice cubes, one with plain water, one with gently steaming warm water.
setup.caption: 1. Fill three glasses: icy, room temperature and warm.

setup.art: A child's hands bending three glow sticks at the same time until they click.
setup.caption: 2. Snap all three glow sticks together. Drop one into each glass.

setup.art: In a dark room, three glasses glowing: the warm one bright, the middle one medium, the icy one dim.
setup.caption: 3. Switch off the light. Which glows brightest?

flow.do: Show your child a glow stick. Do not snap it yet. Ask what they notice.
flow.say: This is a glow stick. Inside is a thin glass tube with one liquid, floating in another liquid. When I bend it, the tube cracks, the liquids mix, and they react. That makes light. A firefly makes light by mixing chemicals too. Do you think warm or cold will make the glow brighter?
flow.kid: Look at the glow stick. Inside are two liquids, kept apart. Bend it and they mix. Then it glows! Guess: brighter in warm water, or in cold?
flow.context: This is the first step of the glow stick test. You find out whether warm or cold water changes how bright a glow stick shines.

flow.do: 1. Put ice and cold water in the first glass. 2. Room-temperature water in the second. 3. Warm water in the third. 4. Fill all three to the same height.
flow.say: Let's fill three glasses to the same height. One icy, one normal, one warm, like a bath. Feel each one with a finger.
flow.kid: Help fill three glasses to the same height. One icy. One normal. One warm, for a grown-up to pour. Feel each with one finger.
flow.parent: Warm enough that you can keep a finger in the water comfortably. Never use boiling water.

flow.do: Snap all three glow sticks at the same moment. Shake them. Drop one into each glass. Wait 2 minutes.
flow.say: On three, we all bend our sticks till they click. One, two, three! Shake them, and drop one in each glass. Now we wait two minutes, so the water can warm or cool them.
flow.kid: Bend all three sticks at once till they click. Shake them. Drop one in each glass. Wait two minutes.
flow.parent: Snapping them together matters. If one started earlier, the test would not be fair.

flow.do: Switch off the light. Look at the three glasses. Rank them 1, 2 and 3 for brightness. Write it in the table.
flow.say: Lights off! Which is brightest? Which is dimmest? Let's give them a number. 1 is the brightest.
flow.kid: Lights off! Look at the three glasses. Which is brightest? Give it a 1. Write it down.

check.q: In the glow stick test, which glass glowed brightest?
options: The warm water
The icy water
They were all exactly the same
check.why: Warmth makes the molecules inside move about faster. They bump into each other more often, so the reaction runs faster and gives out more light each second. Picking 'icy water' may come from thinking cold things shine, like ice glinting. Picking 'the same' may mean the room was not dark enough to see the difference. Try again in a darker room.

flow.do: Put the icy glass, with its stick, in the fridge. Leave the other two on a shelf, out of reach of small children. Next morning, take the icy stick out and look at all three in a dark bathroom straight away.
flow.say: The icy one goes in the fridge, so it stays cold all night. The other two stay out. Tomorrow we will see which one still glows. What do you guess, and why?
flow.kid: Put the icy one in the fridge. Leave the others out. Tomorrow, check all three in the dark.
flow.parent: Party glow sticks usually last several hours at room temperature, so by morning the two on the shelf are often faint or dark. The fridge stick usually glows more clearly, because the cold slowed its reaction all night. This does not always work: if all three are dark or all three still glow, write that down. It is still a result.

check.q: Next morning, which glow stick was most likely still glowing?
options: The one kept cold in the fridge
The one from the warm water
None of them, glow sticks only last a minute
check.why: In the cold, the reaction runs slowly. The stick uses its chemicals slowly, so it lasts longer. The sticks left out used up their chemicals faster. Picking 'warm' usually means thinking brighter means stronger, so it should last longer. In fact, brighter means it is spending its chemicals faster.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Let's put it together. First, what do you think now? Second, what did you see that shows it? Third, why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: warmth makes a glow brighter, and cold makes it last longer. What I saw: the warm stick was brightest, and next morning the fridge one glowed more than the others. Why: warmth makes the chemicals react faster, so they get used up sooner. Fireflies also flash more slowly on cool nights.

experiments.title: Cold Light Test: is a glow hot?
experiments.context: This is the cold light test. You compare a glowing glow stick with one that has not been snapped, and feel whether the light brings any heat. Living light, like a firefly's, is cold light: it makes almost no heat.
experiments.question: Does a glowing glow stick give out heat?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Will the glowing stick feel warmer than the one that is not glowing? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: To make it fair, use two glow sticks from the same packet and let them lie side by side on the same cloth. Press each one on the same place on the inside of your wrist, for the same time, a count of twenty. Then test them again in the other order.
results_table: On my wrist: warmer, cooler or the same as the room?
Thermometer touching it after 2 minutes (degrees), if you have one

materials.item: 2 glow sticks from the same packet
a cloth or tea towel to lay them on
a kitchen or room thermometer, if you have one
extra, only with a grown-up: a diya on a steel plate, and matches

experiments.safety: Never cut or bite a glow stick. If one leaks, wash hands and keep it away from eyes. In the extra step, a grown-up lights and watches the diya all the time.

schedule.what: Compare a glowing and a whole glow stick on your wrist. Measure with a thermometer if you have one. Say what you think, what you felt and why.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw the two glow sticks and write which one felt warmer, or the same.

setup.art: Two glow sticks side by side on a cloth, one snapped and glowing, one whole.
setup.caption: 1. Snap one glow stick. Leave the other whole. Lay them side by side on a cloth.

setup.art: A child pressing the glowing stick against the inside of their wrist, with the whole stick waiting beside.
setup.caption: 2. Press each stick on the inside of your wrist. Count to twenty.

setup.art: Two small thermometers, one touching each glow stick, both showing the same number.
setup.caption: 3. If you have a thermometer, check each stick after 2 minutes.

flow.do: Lay two glow sticks side by side on a cloth. Snap one, shake it, and leave the other whole.
flow.say: One of these makes light and one does not. Both lie on the same cloth in the same room. Do you think the glowing one will feel warmer? A firefly makes light with chemistry too. Does that light bring heat?
flow.kid: One glow stick glows. One does not. Guess: will the glowing one feel warmer?
flow.context: This is the first step of the cold light test. You compare a glowing glow stick with a whole one.

flow.do: Your child presses the glowing stick on the inside of a wrist for a count of twenty. Then the whole stick, for a count of twenty. Then do both again in the other order.
flow.say: Press the glowing one on your wrist. Count to twenty. Now the whole one. Which is warmer? Now try again, the other way round.
flow.kid: Press the glowing stick on your wrist and count to twenty. Now the whole stick. Which felt warmer?

check.q: Which stick felt warmer on your wrist?
options: The one that was glowing
The one that was not glowing
About the same
check.why: A glow stick turns its energy into light and gives out almost no heat. So the glowing stick feels the same as the whole one. That is cold light. Picking 'the glowing one' usually means thinking all light comes with heat, like a bulb or the Sun. If one felt warmer, your wrist may have warmed it; that is why we test both orders.

flow.do: If you have a thermometer, lay it touching each stick for 2 minutes and read it.
flow.say: Feelings can fool us. A thermometer cannot be fooled. Let's measure.
flow.kid: Lay the thermometer touching each stick. Wait two minutes. Read the number.
flow.parent: Both readings should be close to the room temperature. If you have no thermometer, skip this step.

flow.do: Ask for claim, evidence and reasoning.
flow.say: What do you think now? What did you feel or measure? Why do you think a firefly needs cold light?
flow.kid: Say three things. What I think. What I felt. Why a firefly needs cold light.
flow.parent: A good answer: The glow stick makes cold light. The glowing stick felt the same as the whole one. A firefly needs cold light because their light is inside their own body, and a hot light would harm it. Extra, with a grown-up: light a diya on a steel plate and hold a hand one hand-width beside the flame, never above it, for a count of five. A flame gives out a lot of heat as well as light.

experiments.title: Made or Stored? Glow-in-the-dark stars
experiments.context: This test compares glow-in-the-dark stars with living light. A glow-in-the-dark star does not make light. It soaks up light, then gives it back slowly. You test whether shining a torch on it for longer makes it glow for longer.
experiments.question: If we shine a torch on a glow-in-the-dark star for longer, does it glow for longer in the dark?
experiments.predict: Guess. Will a star charged for 60 seconds glow longer than one charged for 10 seconds? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: To make it fair, use two stars from the same packet, side by side. Shine the same torch from the same distance. Change only how long you shine it. Finish charging both at the same moment, and watch both at the same time.
results_table: Minutes until you can no longer see it (stop at 10)

materials.item: 2 glow-in-the-dark stars from the same packet
a torch or a phone torch
a steel bowl or a book, to cover one star
a phone stopwatch or a clock with a seconds hand
a dark room

schedule.what: Keep both stars in the dark for an hour first (this wait is not counted). Charge star A for 10 seconds and star B for 60 seconds, finishing together. Watch which glows brighter and which fades first, for up to 10 minutes.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw two bars, one for each star.

setup.art: Two glow-in-the-dark stars on a table, one under a torch beam, and a phone showing a stopwatch.
setup.caption: 1. Cover star A with a bowl. Shine the torch on star B for 50 seconds. Then lift the bowl and shine on both for 10 more seconds.

setup.art: A dark room with two faintly glowing stars, one brighter than the other, and a child watching.
setup.caption: 2. Switch off all lights. Start the stopwatch.

setup.art: A child pointing at the star that is still glowing while the other has faded.
setup.caption: 3. Note the minute when each star fades away. Stop at 10 minutes.

example_chart.title: Made-up example: how long each star glowed after charging
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up. Your numbers will be different.

flow.do: Keep both stars in a dark drawer for an hour before you start, so they are empty of light.
flow.say: These stars glow in the dark. A firefly makes their own light from food. Do you think these stars make their own light too? Let's find out.
flow.kid: Do glow-in-the-dark stars make their own light, like a firefly? Let's test them.
flow.context: This is the first step of the star test. You find out whether glow-in-the-dark stars make light or just give back light they soaked up.

ask.q: What would happen if we never shone any light on them?
good: Maybe they would still glow a little.

flow.do: Put the two stars side by side. Cover star A with a steel bowl. Shine the torch on star B for 50 seconds. Then lift the bowl and shine on both stars for 10 more seconds. Keep the torch the same distance away.
flow.say: Star A hides under the bowl first. Star B gets fifty seconds of torchlight. Now I lift the bowl, and both get ten more seconds. So star A had ten seconds and star B had sixty, and both finished at the same moment.
flow.kid: Cover star A with a bowl. Shine the torch on star B for 50 seconds. Lift the bowl. Shine on both for 10 more seconds.
flow.parent: Finishing together matters. If star A were charged first, it would already be fading while star B was still being charged.

flow.do: Turn off the lights and start the stopwatch. At 1 minute, say which star is brighter. Then note the minute when each star fades so you cannot see it. Stop at 10 minutes.
flow.say: Lights off. Which star is brighter now? Keep watching. Tell me the moment each one fades away.
flow.kid: Lights off! Which star is brighter? Shout when each one fades away.

check.q: Star A and star B glow about the same at 1 minute. Did the test fail?
options: No. The stars may fill up with light quickly, and that is a real result
Yes. The stars must be broken
Yes. The torch was not on
check.why: A test does not fail when the result is a surprise. Some glow-in-the-dark stars fill up with light after only a few seconds, so a longer torch time adds nothing. Picking 'broken' or 'torch not on' skips the idea that the answer 'no difference' is still an answer.

flow.parent: Some stars fade in a few minutes. Others glow faintly for much longer. If a star still glows at 10 minutes, write 'more than 10'. Some stars fill up with light very fast, so both may glow the same. If so, write that down. It is a real result: 10 seconds was already enough.

flow.do: Compare with a firefly. Ask for claim, evidence and reasoning.
flow.say: A firefly glows in the darkest night, with no torch at all. A star only gives back light it soaked up. What do you think now? What did you see? Why?
flow.kid: A firefly needs no torch. A star does. Say three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: A good answer: The stars do not make their own light. They glowed only after the torch had shone on them, so they give back light they soaked up. A firefly is different, because they make new light from food and oxygen.

activities.title: Snap! A light with no switch
activities.context: This is a short way into the unit. In a dark room, you snap a glow stick and notice everything you can about its light. It works a bit like a firefly.

materials.item: 1 glow stick
a room you can make dark

activities.safety: Never cut or bite a glow stick.

schedule.what: Snap a glow stick in the dark. Notice and wonder.

activities.record: Write or say three things you noticed and two things you wonder.

setup.art: A child in a dark room holding an unsnapped glow stick in both hands.
setup.caption: 1. Make the room dark. Hold the glow stick.

setup.art: The glow stick bending with a small click, light spreading along it.
setup.caption: 2. Bend it till it clicks. Shake it.

setup.art: The child holding the glowing stick up and looking around the dark room, eyes wide.
setup.caption: 3. Look around by its light. What can you see?

flow.do: Make the room dark. Hand your child the glow stick, not yet snapped.
flow.say: Here's a stick with no battery, no wire and no flame. Let's see if it can make light.
flow.kid: Hold the stick. It has no battery and no wire. Can it make light?
flow.context: This is the first step of Snap!, a quick look at a light that needs no switch.

flow.do: Your child bends the stick till it clicks, then shakes it.
flow.say: Bend it till you hear a click. Shake it. What do you notice?
flow.kid: Bend it till it clicks. Shake it. What happens?

good: It got brighter when I shook it.

flow.do: Ask your child to hold the glowing stick up and look around the room by its light.
flow.say: Look around the room. What can you see by its light? Hold it close to something, then far away. What changes?
flow.kid: Look around the room by its glow. Hold it close to something, then far away. What changes?

check.q: You bent the glow stick and it began to glow. What made the light?
options: Two liquids inside mixed and reacted
A tiny battery hidden inside
The warmth of your hands
check.why: Bending cracks a thin glass tube inside, so two liquids mix and react. The reaction gives out light. There is no battery or wire. Picking 'the warmth of your hands' may come from thinking light needs heat. A glow stick makes light without getting hot.

flow.do: Ask what your child wonders. Write down every question.
flow.say: What do you wonder about this light? Any question is a good question.
flow.kid: What do you wonder? Say every question you have.
flow.parent: Good wonderings: Where does the light come from? Will it run out? Can living things do this? Keep the list. The unit will answer many of them.

activities.title: Firefly Night Walk (if you live near a park, field or garden)
activities.context: This is a night walk to look for fireflies, small beetles that flash light. Do it only if a park, field or garden with dark corners is near you, because fireflies are rare in brightly lit city areas. You count flashes for one minute in a dark spot and near a bright light.

materials.item: a torch with a red cloth or red cellophane over it
a phone stopwatch or a watch
paper and pencil for tally marks

activities.safety: Go only with a grown-up. Wear closed shoes and long trousers. Watch for snakes near grass and water. Do not catch the fireflies.

schedule.what: After sunset, walk to a dark garden, park or field. Count flashes for one minute in two places.

activities.record: Make tally marks of flashes. Write the place and the time. Draw one firefly you saw.

setup.art: A grown-up and a child at the edge of a dark field at dusk, the torch covered with red cloth.
setup.caption: 1. Go out after sunset with a grown-up. Cover the torch with red cloth.

setup.art: A child making tally marks on paper while tiny flashes dot the dark grass.
setup.caption: 2. Stand still for one minute. Make a tally mark for each flash.

setup.art: The same child near a bright lamp post, with only one or two flashes in the dark beyond.
setup.caption: 3. Count again for one minute near a bright light. Compare.

flow.do: Choose a dark place: a garden, a park, a field edge. Go after sunset. Cover your torch with red cloth.
flow.say: We're going firefly spotting. We'll keep our torch dim and red, so our light doesn't drown theirs.
flow.kid: Go out with a grown-up after sunset. Keep the torch dim and red. Bright light hides firefly flashes.
flow.context: This is the first step of the firefly night walk. Fireflies are most common on warm, damp nights before and during the monsoon.
flow.parent: In much of India, fireflies are easiest to see from late May to July, around the first rains. If you see none, that is a real result too. Write it down. If there is no dark green place near you, play Flash and Answer instead.

flow.do: Stand still in the darkest spot for one minute. Your child makes a tally mark for every flash.
flow.say: Let's stand very still. For one minute, make a mark for every flash you see.
flow.kid: Stand still. For one minute, make a mark for each flash.

flow.do: Walk to a spot near a bright street light or porch light. Count for one minute again.
flow.say: Now let's try right next to the bright light. Count again for one minute.
flow.kid: Now count again near a bright light. One minute.

check.q: Where did you probably count more firefly flashes?
options: In the dark spot
Next to the bright light
Always exactly the same in both
check.why: Fireflies flash to find each other. Near bright lights, their flashes are hard to see, and many fireflies stop flashing or move away. Picking 'next to the bright light' may come from moths, which fly to lamps. Fireflies are different. If your counts were the same, that is fine. Try on another night.

flow.do: Watch one firefly closely. Do they flash in a pattern? Are they flying or sitting still?
flow.say: Let's watch just one firefly. How many flashes in a row? How long between them?
flow.kid: Watch one firefly. Count their flashes. Are they flying, or sitting on a leaf?
flow.parent: Flying ones are often males, flashing their code. Ones sitting low on leaves are often females, answering.

flow.do: At home, ask for claim, evidence and reasoning.
flow.say: What do you think about fireflies and bright lights? What did you count? Why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say three things. What I think. What I counted. Why.
flow.parent: A good answer: Bright lights are bad for fireflies. I counted 14 flashes in the dark spot and 2 near the lamp. Fireflies can't see each other's flashes in bright light.

activities.title: Shoebox Deep Sea
activities.context: In this activity you make a model of the deep sea inside a dark shoebox. The deep sea is the part of the ocean that sunlight never reaches. You add creatures that make their own light.

materials.item: a shoebox with a lid
black paper or paint
glow-in-the-dark paint or small glow-in-the-dark stars
white card, scissors, thread and sticky tape

activities.safety: A grown-up helps with the scissors and makes the peephole.

schedule.what: Paint the box black. Make deep-sea creatures. Add their lights. Look through the peephole in the dark.

activities.record: Label each creature with their light job: catch, hide, scare or talk.

setup.art: A shoebox lying on its side, painted black inside, with a small hole cut in one end.
setup.caption: 1. Paint the inside of the box black. A grown-up cuts a peephole.

setup.art: Cut-out card fish, jellyfish and an anglerfish hanging on threads, with dots of glow paint on them.
setup.caption: 2. Make creatures from card. Paint only their light spots with glow paint.

setup.art: An eye at the peephole, and inside the box tiny glowing dots and a glowing anglerfish lure.
setup.caption: 3. Charge the paint with a torch, close the lid and peep in.

flow.do: Line the inside of the box and lid with black paper, or paint them black and let the paint dry. A grown-up cuts a coin-sized peephole in one end.
flow.say: Deep in the sea, below about a thousand metres, it is black all day and all night. Let's make that darkness in a box.
flow.kid: Line the inside of the box with black paper, or paint it black. That is the deep sea. Ask a grown-up to cut a small peephole.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Shoebox Deep Sea. You build a dark sea in a box and fill it with glowing creatures.

flow.do: Your child draws and cuts out 3 to 5 deep-sea animals. Paint glow paint, or stick a small glow star, only where each animal makes light.
flow.say: Let's make an anglerfish, a jellyfish and a hatchetfish. Where does each one glow? Paint only those parts.
flow.kid: Make 3 to 5 sea creatures from card. Paint glow dots only where each one glows.
flow.parent: The anglerfish glows on the ball dangling in front of their mouth. The hatchetfish glows along their belly. A jellyfish can glow in a ring. Lanternfish have rows of dots along their sides.

flow.do: Hang the creatures from the lid with thread and tape. Shine a torch on them for a minute, then close the box.
flow.say: Let's hang them up. Now give them a minute of torchlight to charge the paint.
flow.kid: Hang them from the lid with thread. Shine a torch on them. Close the lid.
flow.parent: Wait for any paint to dry before you hang the animals.

flow.do: Your child looks in through the peephole in a dark room.
flow.say: Peep in. What can you see? What can't you see?
flow.kid: Look through the hole. You can only see the glowing parts!

check.q: Our paint glows because we shone a torch on it. Real deep-sea animals have no torch. Where does their light come from?
options: They make it with chemistry in their bodies
From sunlight reaching the deep sea
From the Moon
check.why: Deep-sea animals make light with luciferin and oxygen, or with glowing bacteria they keep. Our paint only stores torchlight. Picking 'sunlight' misses that sunlight never reaches the deep sea. Picking 'the Moon' misses that moonlight is only sunlight bounced off the Moon, and it cannot reach the deep sea either.

flow.parent: Glow paint and glow stars are faint. Wait a minute in the dark for your eyes to adjust. The glow fades after some minutes; open the lid and shine the torch again to recharge it.

activities.title: The Vanishing Fish: hiding with belly lights
activities.context: This activity shows how some sea animals hide by glowing. Seen from below, a fish looks like a dark shape against the light from above. A light on their belly can make that shape disappear.

materials.item: a fish shape cut from thin white paper, about the size of your palm
a phone or tablet showing a plain white screen, turned to low brightness
a small torch, or a second phone's torch

schedule.what: Hold a paper fish against a glowing screen. Make its shape vanish with a torch from the front.

activities.record: Draw the fish before and after. Write: from below, a dark fish shows up because...

setup.art: A paper fish held flat against a dim glowing white screen in a dark room, showing as a darker shape.
setup.caption: 1. Hold the paper fish flat on a dim glowing screen. See its dark shape.

setup.art: A child shining a small torch onto the front of the same paper fish.
setup.caption: 2. Shine a small torch on the front of the fish.

setup.art: The paper fish almost invisible against the screen, the outline barely there.
setup.caption: 3. Move the torch nearer or further until the fish nearly vanishes.

flow.do: In a dim room, put the phone on a table with a white screen at low brightness. Lay the paper fish flat on the screen. Look from straight above.
flow.say: Pretend you are a hungry fish deep in the sea, looking up. The screen is the faint light from far above. What does our little fish look like?
flow.kid: Look down at the fish on the screen. You are a hungry fish looking up. Can you see the little fish?
flow.context: This is the first step of The Vanishing Fish. You find out how a fish can hide by glowing on their belly.

flow.do: Your child shines the torch onto the fish from above. Move it closer or further until the fish is as bright as the screen.
flow.say: Now let's give our fish belly lights. Shine the torch on it. Move the torch until the fish matches the screen.
flow.kid: Shine the torch on the fish. Move it closer or further. Can you make the fish disappear?

check.q: Why did the fish nearly disappear?
options: It became just as bright as the light behind it
The torch made it see-through
The fish moved away
check.why: We see a shape when it is darker or brighter than what is behind it. When the fish matches the background, the outline is gone. Real hatchetfish make their belly glow just as bright as the light from above. Picking 'see-through' is a good guess, but the paper did not change. Only its brightness did.

flow.do: Talk about real animals.
flow.say: In the sea, a fish with belly lights is hard to spot from below. A hunter looking up sees no dark shape, so they swim on.
flow.kid: Real hatchetfish do this. Their bellies glow. Hunters below can't see them.
flow.think: On land, a light shows people where you are. Why is it different in the dark sea?

flow.do: Ask for claim, evidence and reasoning.
flow.say: What do you think now? What did you see? Why?
flow.kid: Say three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: A good answer: Belly lights help a fish hide. Our paper fish nearly vanished when the torch made the paper as bright as the screen. A hunter below can't see a shape that matches the light above.

activities.title: Deep Sea Theatre: act out the glowing jobs
activities.context: This is a short play in a dim room. Family members act as deep-sea animals and use torches or glow sticks for their lights. Deep-sea animals glow to catch food, hide, scare attackers and talk.

materials.item: 2 or 3 glow sticks or small torches
a dim room
string

activities.safety: Never cut or bite a glow stick.

schedule.what: Act out three short deep-sea scenes with lights.

setup.art: A family in a dim living room, one person holding a glow stick on a string in front of their face like an anglerfish lure.
setup.caption: 1. Scene 1: the anglerfish dangles their lure. A small fish swims close.

setup.art: A child crouched low, holding a glow stick under their tummy, while a grown-up looks up from the floor.
setup.caption: 2. Scene 2: the hidden fish glows on their belly.

setup.art: A child whirling a glow stick in a circle while a 'shrimp' tiptoes away.
setup.caption: 3. Scene 3: the jellyfish flashes their burglar alarm.

flow.do: Scene 1. One person is an anglerfish, dangling a glow stick on a string in front of their mouth. Another is a small fish.
flow.say: The anglerfish waits in the dark, very still. Only their lure glows. Little fish, swim towards the light!
flow.kid: Be a little fish. You see a light! Swim close. Oh no, it's an anglerfish!
flow.context: This is the first step of Deep Sea Theatre. You act out how deep-sea animals use light.

flow.do: Scene 2. One person lies on the floor as a hunter looking up. Another walks past holding a glow stick under their belly.
flow.say: Hunter, look up. Can you see the shape of the fish going past? The fish is glowing on their belly to hide.
flow.kid: Hold the glow stick under your tummy. Walk past the hunter. Glowing helps you hide!

flow.do: Scene 3. One person is a jellyfish. Another is a hungry shrimp who grabs the jellyfish. The jellyfish whirls their glow stick in a circle. The shrimp gets frightened that a bigger fish may come, and runs.
flow.say: The jellyfish is caught! They flash a ring of lights. That may call a bigger fish. Shrimp, run!
flow.kid: You are a jellyfish. When the shrimp grabs you, spin your light in a circle. Call for help!

check.q: In scene 3, why does the jellyfish flash when they are grabbed?
options: The flashes may call a bigger hunter to eat the attacker
To light up their dinner
To say hello to their friends
check.why: Scientists call this a burglar alarm. The flashes may bring a bigger animal that eats the shrimp. Picking 'light up their dinner' mixes it up with a lure. Picking 'say hello' mixes it up with talking signals. Each glow has its own job.

flow.do: Swap roles and play the scene each of you liked best.
flow.say: Which job did your light have in each scene? Catch, hide or scare?
flow.kid: Swap parts. Say which job your light had.

projects.title: Firefly Count for Science (if you live near a park, field or garden)
projects.context: In this 3-night project, you count fireflies in the same place, at the same time, on three evenings. It needs a park, field or garden with dark corners near you. Scientists need counts like this to know if fireflies are disappearing.

materials.item: a notebook for a firefly diary
a phone stopwatch or a watch
a torch covered with red cloth

projects.safety: Go only with a grown-up. Wear closed shoes. Stay on paths, away from water edges.

schedule.what: Choose a spot and mark it. Count flashes for 3 minutes, 30 minutes after sunset. Write the weather.
Same spot, same time. Count for 3 minutes. Write the weather. Ask an older neighbour or relative, if you have one, how many fireflies they saw as a child.
Count again. Make a bar chart of your three nights. Write a short report.

projects.record: Each night write the date, time, weather and your count. On night 3, draw a bar chart.

setup.art: A child and a parent marking a spot with a stone at the edge of a garden at dusk.
setup.caption: 1. Choose one spot and mark it. Come back at the same time each night.

setup.art: A child with a notebook and stopwatch, making tally marks, tiny flashes in the bushes.
setup.caption: 2. Count flashes for 3 minutes. Write the weather.

setup.art: A notebook page with three bars for three nights, and an older neighbour pointing at it.
setup.caption: 3. After 3 nights, draw a bar chart. Ask an older neighbour what they remember.

flow.do: Choose a dark spot near home where you might see fireflies. Mark it. Decide the time: about 30 minutes after sunset.
flow.say: Scientists want to know if fireflies are disappearing. To find out, they need careful counts. We can help. We'll count in the same place, at the same time, for three nights.
flow.kid: You are a firefly scientist. Pick one spot. Come back at the same time for three nights.
flow.context: This is the first step of the firefly count project. You count fireflies on three nights to see how their numbers change.
flow.parent: Same place and same time make the counts fair. The best season is late May to July. If you see no fireflies at all, record zero. A zero is also data.

flow.do: Each night, count flashes for 3 minutes. Write the count, the weather and whether the Moon was out.
flow.say: Three minutes, starting now. Mark every flash. Is it warm or cool tonight? Is it damp?
flow.kid: Count every flash for 3 minutes. Write the number. Is it warm, cool, wet or dry?
flow.wait: Repeat on the next two evenings

flow.do: On night 3, draw a bar chart with one bar for each night.
flow.say: Let's draw a bar for each night. Which night had the most? What was different that night?
flow.kid: Draw one bar for each night. Which night had the most flashes? Why, do you think?

chart.title: Made-up example: firefly flashes counted in 3 minutes
chart.note: These numbers are made up. Your numbers will be different.

check.q: In this made-up example from the firefly count, which night had the most flashes?
options: Night 3, after rain
Night 2, cool and windy
All nights were the same
check.why: Night 3 has the tallest bar, 31 flashes. Fireflies are often busier on warm, damp nights. Picking night 2 may mean reading the shortest bar as the biggest. The taller the bar, the more flashes.

flow.do: Ask a grandparent, relative or neighbour who has lived here long how many fireflies they saw as a child.
flow.say: Let's ask someone who has lived here a long time. Were there more fireflies when you were young? Where did you see them?
flow.kid: Ask someone older. Did they see more fireflies when they were small? Where?
flow.parent: Many people say there were more fireflies before. Memories are useful clues, but they are not careful counts. That is why your counts matter.
flow.think: Is someone's memory good evidence? How could we find out for sure if fireflies are disappearing?

flow.do: Write a short report: where, when, what you counted and what you think.
flow.say: Let's write a short science report. What do you think? What did you count? Why?
flow.kid: Write your report. What I think. What I counted. Why.
flow.parent: A good report: Fireflies like warm, damp nights. I counted 31 flashes after the rain and 9 on the cool windy night. Fireflies may flash more when it is warm and wet. Firefly scientists around the world collect counts like these. Ask if a local nature group collects them.

challenges.title: Invent a Deep-Sea Creature
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. You invent a new animal for the dark deep sea. They must use their own light to catch food without being eaten.
challenges.problem: Design an animal that lives 2,000 metres down, in always-dark water. They must find food and stay safe, using light they make themself.
constraints: Their light must be cold light, made by chemistry, not fire.
They may glow in no more than three places.
Each light must have a job: catch, hide, scare or talk.
No sunlight reaches them, so every light must be made by the animal.
materials: a glow stick or glow paint, for a model
clay or card, if you want to build it
general: Give them a glowing lure near their mouth, like an anglerfish.
Give them belly lights to hide their shape from hunters below.
Let them squirt glowing liquid to escape, like some shrimp.
creative: Give them lights that blink in a code only their own kind knows.
Let them keep glowing bacteria in a pocket, and switch them off with a flap of skin, like a flashlight fish.
Let them flash a burglar alarm that calls a bigger hunter.
challenges.your_turn: Now draw your own creature. Give them a name. Label each light and its job. Then build it from clay or card, and look at it in a dark shoebox or a dark room.

setup.art: A sheet of paper with a sketch of an odd fish, and small arrows pointing to three glowing spots.
setup.caption: 1. Draw your creature. Mark where they glow.

setup.art: Labels next to each glowing spot, shown as small pictures: a fish hook, an eye with a slash, a lightning bolt, two speech bubbles.
setup.caption: 2. Give each light a job: catch, hide, scare or talk.

setup.art: A clay model of the creature with glow-paint spots inside a dark shoebox.
setup.caption: 3. Build it and look at it in the dark.

flow.do: Read the problem together. Talk about the four jobs light can do in the deep sea.
flow.say: Down at 2,000 metres, it is black all the time. Your animal needs food and needs to stay safe. Their only tool is light they make themself.
flow.kid: Your animal lives deep in the dark sea. They need food. They must not be eaten. They can glow.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Invent a Deep-Sea Creature challenge. You design an animal that uses their own light.

flow.do: Your child draws the creature and marks up to three lights.
flow.say: Draw your creature. Where will they glow? Remember, no more than three lights.
flow.kid: Draw your animal. Mark up to three glowing spots.

flow.do: For each light, your child says or writes its job and how it works.
flow.say: Tell me about each light. Is it for catching, hiding, scaring or talking? How does it work?
flow.kid: For each light, say its job. Catch, hide, scare or talk? How does it work?

check.q: Your creature has bright lights all over their back. A hunter swims below them. Are they well hidden?
options: Not really. Belly lights hide you from hunters below
Yes, back lights hide you from below
Light can never help hiding
check.why: Hunters below see your underside against the faint light from above. So hiding lights must be on the belly. Back lights would show to hunters above. Picking 'light can never help hiding' is natural on land. In the deep sea, belly lights are a real way to hide.

flow.do: Build it if there is time, and test it in the dark.
flow.say: Let's build it and switch off the lights. Does it look the way you hoped?
flow.kid: Build your animal. Test it in the dark. What would you change?

challenges.title: Light the Path, Save the Fireflies
challenges.context: This is a design challenge about light pollution. Light pollution is too much light at night where it is not needed. It stops fireflies from finding each other.
challenges.problem: A path through a park needs light, so people can walk home safely at night. But fireflies live in the park. Design lighting that keeps people safe and leaves the fireflies in the dark.
constraints: People must be able to see the path and their feet.
The fireflies' bushes and grass must stay as dark as possible.
Test your design on a model with torches and a toy path.
materials: a strip of paper for a path, on the floor
paper cups, foil or card to make shades
a few glow-in-the-dark stars or glow sticks, for 'fireflies'
general: Use shades so lights point down at the path only.
Use fewer, dimmer lights, low to the ground.
Switch lights off late at night, or use lights that turn on only when someone walks by.
creative: Mark the path edges with glow-in-the-dark stones or paint that need no electricity.
Use warm, dim lamps instead of bright white ones.
Leave a dark 'firefly corner' in every park.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own park lighting. Draw it. Build it with cups and torches. Can you keep the path bright and the firefly corner dark?

setup.art: A paper path on a dark floor with glow-in-the-dark stars scattered in a 'bush' area beside it.
setup.caption: 1. Lay out a paper path and a firefly bush with glowing stars.

setup.art: A torch shining sideways and flooding the whole area, stars no longer visible.
setup.caption: 2. Shine an open torch. Can you still see the 'fireflies'?

setup.art: A torch inside a paper cup shade, pointing straight down at the path, stars glowing again in the dark beside it.
setup.caption: 3. Add a shade so light points only down at the path.

flow.do: Lay out the paper path and put the glow stars a little way beside it, as fireflies. Shine a torch on the stars for 30 seconds to charge them. Then darken the room.
flow.say: These glowing stars are our fireflies. The paper is a path. People need light to walk here. Fireflies need dark to see each other.
flow.kid: The stars are fireflies. The paper is a path. People need light. Fireflies need dark.
flow.context: This is the first step of Light the Path. You design lights that keep a path safe without hurting fireflies.

flow.do: Hold an unshaded torch above the path, shining all around. Look at the fireflies.
flow.say: Here's an ordinary lamp. What happens to our fireflies?
flow.kid: Shine the torch all around. Can you still see the fireflies?

check.q: In the Light the Path test, the open torch lit up everything. What happened to the 'fireflies'?
options: They became hard to see
They glowed brighter
Nothing changed
check.why: A bright light around them drowns out their faint glow. Real fireflies are harmed the same way, because they cannot see each other's flashes. Picking 'glowed brighter' may come from glow stars charging up in light. But we cannot see them while the torch floods the area.

flow.do: Your child designs shades from cups, foil or card, and tests them.
flow.say: Make a shade so the light only lands on the path. Test it. Can you see the fireflies now?
flow.kid: Make a shade from a cup or card. Point the light down. Test it.

flow.do: Compare designs and pick the best.
flow.say: Which design kept the path brightest and the firefly bush darkest? Why?
flow.kid: Which design worked best? Why?
flow.think: Where near our home is there a light that shines where nobody needs it?

videos.title: The weird, wonderful world of bioluminescence
videos.why: Edith Widder, a deep-sea scientist, shows real film of glowing animals and explains the four jobs of living light. Good for the parent, and gripping for children.
videos.check: Title and channel confirmed on YouTube.

videos.title: Fireflies: Nature's Femme Fatales
videos.why: Shows firefly flash codes, and the trickster females that copy another kind's answer to catch males.
videos.check: Title and channel confirmed on YouTube.

videos.title: Beach glows as glowing plankton shows up
videos.why: A short news film of waves glowing blue in Australia. The same kind of glow is seen on some nights on Indian beaches, such as Juhu in Mumbai and beaches near Chennai and Goa.
videos.check: Title and channel confirmed on YouTube.

quiz.p: Which of these is living light?
opts: A glow stick at a wedding
quiz.why: Living light is made by a living being. A glow stick uses the same kind of chemistry, but nobody alive is making it. A glow-in-the-dark star only gives back stored light.

quiz.p: A jellyfish glows in a fish tank in a room with every light switched off. Is that living light?
opts: Yes, because there is no other light for the jellyfish to send back
No, the jellyfish is only sending back light
No, the water in the tank is glowing
quiz.why: In a fully dark room there is no light to bounce back. So any glow must be made by the jellyfish themself, with chemistry. That is living light. Picking 'sending back light' forgets that the room is dark.

quiz.p: Where do glowing mushrooms usually grow?
opts: On rotting wood in damp forests
quiz.why: Glowing fungi grow on damp, rotting wood, like the fallen bamboo near Mawlynnong in Meghalaya. Picking 'deep sea' mixes them up with glowing fish.

quiz.p: Where on Earth do the most glowing animals live?
opts: In the sea, especially the deep sea
quiz.why: In the deep sea, about three out of four animals can make light. Picking 'cities' may come from all the lamps there, but those are not living lights.

quiz.p: On some nights, the waves on beaches near Chennai and Mangaluru glow blue. What makes the glow?
opts: Tiny living beings in the water called sea sparkle
quiz.why: Sea sparkle are tiny one-celled living beings. They flash blue when the water is stirred. Moonlight on waves is silver and does not flash.

quiz.p: A scientist mixes luciferin and luciferase, the two firefly chemicals, in a sealed tube with no air in it. What happens?
opts: No light, because there is no oxygen
A bright flash, because both chemicals are there
A slow glow that gets hot
quiz.why: Luciferin needs oxygen to react. The luciferase only speeds the reaction up. With no oxygen, nothing reacts, so no light comes out. Let air in, and the tube glows. Picking 'a bright flash' forgets the oxygen.

quiz.p: A firefly's light goes off. What has the firefly stopped doing?
quiz.why: Without fresh oxygen from the air, the reaction stops and so does the light. A firefly can sit still and still flash.

quiz.p: A firefly flashes a code to find a partner. Which job of living light is that?
quiz.why: Living light has four main jobs: talking, catching food, hiding and scaring off an attacker. A flash code is a message, so it is talking.

quiz.p: A small squid in Hawaii keeps glowing bacteria under their body. On moonlit nights the glow hides their shadow from hunters below. Which job is that?
quiz.why: The glow fills in the dark shadow, so hunters below cannot see the squid. That is hiding.

quiz.p: To make the glow stick test fair, what must be different between the glasses?
opts: Only how warm the water is
The colour of each glow stick
quiz.why: A fair test changes just one thing. If the colours were different too, we would not know what caused the change. Picking 'everything' is a common first idea, but then we could never tell which change mattered.

quiz.p: A glow-in-the-dark star stops glowing after a while. Why?
opts: It has given back all the light it soaked up
quiz.why: Glow-in-the-dark stars only store light. When the stored light is used up, they go dark until a light charges them again. Picking 'ran out of oxygen' mixes it up with living light, which needs oxygen.

quiz.p: A glow-in-the-dark star and a living firefly both spend a whole day in a dark cupboard. Then you open the door at night. Which one can still glow?
quiz.why: The star can only give back light it soaked up, and it got none in the cupboard. The firefly makes new light with chemistry, so they can flash after a day in the dark. Picking 'only the star' gets the two the wrong way round.

quiz.p: What do bright lights at night do to fireflies?
opts: Hide their flashes, so they find fewer partners
quiz.why: Bright lights drown out faint firefly flashes. Picking 'help them see' may come from moths, which fly to lights. Fireflies are different.

opts: Scientists are still not sure. One idea is that the glow brings insects that spread spores
quiz.why: For one Brazilian mushroom, tests show the glow brings insects. For most other fungi, nobody knows yet. Picking 'to find partners' fits fireflies, who signal to their own kind, not fungi.

applications: Glow sticks, used for safety at night, in camping, at sea and at celebrations, work by the same kind of chemistry as fireflies.
Hospitals and food factories use firefly chemicals in swab tests. The swab glows if germs or food bits are left on a surface.
Scientists attach the green glowing protein from a jellyfish to parts of cells, to watch them grow and move.
Doctors and scientists use glowing chemicals to test new medicines on cells in the lab.
Engineers copied the shape of tiny scales on a firefly's lantern, to help more light escape from LED lights.
Scientists have put mushroom glow genes into plants, which glow faintly. One day, plants might light paths.
Glowing bacteria are used to test whether water has harmful chemicals in it. If the bacteria dim, something is poisoning them.
Deep-sea scientists use fake glowing lures, like Edith Widder's e-jelly, to bring shy animals to their cameras.
Sailors have long known that glowing plankton can show the trail of a ship or a submarine at night.
Firefly festivals in Maharashtra bring visitors and money to villages that protect their forests.
Lighting designers make park and beach lights that point down and stay dim, to protect fireflies and turtles.
Glow-in-the-dark exit signs and paint help people find their way out in a power cut.

open_questions.q: How does a firefly switch their light on and off so fast?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists know oxygen is let in and shut off. Exactly how the firefly controls this in a fraction of a second is still argued about.

open_questions.q: How do thousands of fireflies flash at exactly the same moment?
open_questions.why_open: Each firefly seems to watch their neighbours and adjust. Scientists build computer models, but how real fireflies do it is not fully known.

open_questions.q: Why do most glowing mushrooms glow?
open_questions.why_open: For one Brazilian mushroom, the glow brings insects. For many others, nobody has tested it.

open_questions.q: How did living light first begin in each group of living things?
open_questions.why_open: It began separately many times. Nobody was there to see, and old glowing animals rarely leave fossils that show their light.

open_questions.q: How many kinds of glowing animals live in the deep sea?
open_questions.why_open: Most of the deep sea has never been visited. New glowing animals are found on almost every deep trip.

open_questions.q: Are India's fireflies disappearing, and how fast?
open_questions.why_open: There are very few long, careful counts of fireflies in India. Scientists need many more people counting, in the same places, year after year.

open_questions.q: Does the faint light given off by our bodies tell us anything useful about health?
open_questions.why_open: It has been measured, but it is so faint that scientists are only beginning to study it.

maths.problem: In the made-up firefly count, these were the flashes counted in 3 minutes: Night 1, 24. Night 2, 9. Night 3, 31. Look at the chart. Put the nights in order, from most flashes to fewest.
maths.explain: Compare the numbers. 31 is bigger than 24, and 24 is bigger than 9. So Night 3 had the most, then Night 1, then Night 2. On the chart, the tallest bar is Night 3 and the shortest is Night 2.
maths.context: This is about the firefly count project. You count firefly flashes for 3 minutes, at the same place and time, on three nights.

chart.title: Made-up example: firefly flashes counted in 3 minutes

maths.why_maths: A list of counts is hard to read. Putting them in order shows straight away which night the fireflies liked best.

maths.problem: On the night walk, you counted 12 firefly flashes in 1 minute in the dark spot, and 3 flashes in 1 minute next to a bright lamp. How many times more flashes did you see in the dark?
maths.explain: In the dark spot there were 12 flashes. Near the lamp there were 3. 12 divided by 3 is 4. You can check: 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 = 12. So there were 4 times as many flashes in the dark.
maths.context: This is about the firefly night walk. You counted firefly flashes for one minute in a dark place, then one minute near a bright light.

chart.title: Made-up example: flashes counted in 1 minute

maths.why_maths: Saying '4 times more' tells us how big the effect of a bright light is, not just that there is one.

maths.problem: A firefly flashes once every 5 seconds. How many times do they flash in 1 minute?
maths.explain: One minute is 60 seconds. The firefly flashes once in every group of 5 seconds. 60 divided into groups of 5 makes 12 groups. Or count in fives: 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 35, 40, 45, 50, 55, 60. That is 12 fives. So they flash 12 times.
maths.context: In many kinds of fireflies, the male flashes his code again and again, with the same gap each time. You watched this on the firefly night walk.
maths.why_maths: Counting in equal groups lets a scientist work out a firefly's flash rate without counting for a whole minute.

maths.problem: In the made-up star test results, star A glowed for 3 minutes after 10 seconds of torchlight. Star B glowed for 7 minutes after 60 seconds of torchlight. Look at the chart. How many minutes longer did star B glow? How many seconds is that?
maths.explain: Star B glowed for 7 minutes. Star A glowed for 3 minutes. 7 take away 3 is 4. One minute is 60 seconds, and 60 + 60 + 60 + 60 = 240. So star B glowed 4 minutes, or 240 seconds, longer.
maths.context: This is about the star test. You shone a torch on two glow-in-the-dark stars for different times, then timed how long each one glowed in the dark.

chart.title: Made-up example: how long each star glowed

maths.why_maths: Finding the difference between two times tells us how much the extra torchlight helped.

maths.problem: Sunlight fades as it goes down into the sea. At 200 metres it is dim. Below 1,000 metres it is completely dark. An anglerfish lives at 2,000 metres. How many metres below the start of the total darkness are they?
maths.explain: Total darkness starts at about 1,000 metres. The anglerfish lives at 2,000 metres. 2,000 take away 1,000 is 1,000. So they live 1,000 metres below where the last light ends. That is about as deep as ten football fields laid end to end.
maths.context: This is about the deep sea, the part of the ocean that sunlight never reaches. You built a model of it in the Shoebox Deep Sea.

chart.title: How deep: from the dim sea to the anglerfish

maths.why_maths: Big numbers like thousands of metres are hard to picture. Subtracting them tells us how far into the dark the anglerfish really lives.

warmup.q: Name one living thing that glows, apart from a firefly.

warmup.q: Why does an anglerfish have a glowing lure?

warmup.q: Does a glow-in-the-dark star make its own light?

warmup.q: Name one thing that helps fireflies at night.
warmup.a: Fewer and dimmer lights, pointed down at the path, and switched off when nobody needs them.

warmup.q: Does a glow stick glow brighter or dimmer in warm water?
warmup.a: Brighter, but it runs out sooner.

roots.context: We have been learning about living light: fireflies, mushrooms and sea animals that make their own glow. Now we ask what that tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: The glow stick in warm water shone brightest. A stick kept cold overnight usually still glows next morning. All of them began with the same chemicals, and warmth only made them react faster. So how bright a light is shows how fast it is using up its store of energy.
deep_truth.habit: We think a brighter light is a stronger light, with more inside it. The glow stick test shows that brightness is about speed: the same store, spent quickly or slowly.
deep_truth.evidence: In the glow stick test, the warm stick shone brightest. The stick kept cold in the fridge shone dimmer, but usually glowed longest. Fireflies also flash more slowly on cool nights.

three.who_am_i: Your body runs on chemistry too. It even gives out a faint light, far too weak for your eyes to see.
three.what_is_life: A firefly turns energy from their food into flashes, and uses them to find a partner in the dark.
three.what_is_this_world: Sunlight never reaches the deep sea. Almost all the light down there is made by living things.

roots.thread: Plants catch sunlight and store its energy as food. Firefly young eat snails and worms, which fed on plants. Some of that stored energy later leaves the firefly as a flash. The glow stick test showed that a store of energy can come out fast and bright, or slow and dim. At every step the energy changes form, but it is never destroyed.

science.text: Living light comes from a chemical reaction of luciferin with oxygen. The energy in the food that powers it first came from sunlight caught by plants.
Living light began separately at least 94 times in the history of life. Scientists worked this out by comparing family trees of living things.

other_view.view: A firefly's glow is chemistry that helped fireflies survive and have young. It needs no deeper meaning. There is no One behind it, only molecules and evolution. That is an honest and careful view.

how_we_found_out.story: For thousands of years, people saw rotting wood and old fish glowing in the dark. Many thought the glow was a slow, cool kind of fire, or sunlight the wood had stored. In the 1660s, the English scientist Robert Boyle tested it. He put glowing wood inside a glass jar and pumped the air out. The glow faded away. When he let the air back in, the glow came back. So the light needed air, as a flame does. But the wood stayed cold, and nothing was burning. Later, scientists found that the glow came from fungi living in the wood. In the 1880s, the French scientist Raphael Dubois took the glowing parts of a click beetle. He soaked some in cold water. That liquid glowed for a while, then went dark. He soaked others in very hot water, which stopped the glow at once. Then he mixed the two dark liquids, and the light came back. The heat had destroyed a helper chemical but left the fuel unharmed. He named the fuel luciferin and the helper luciferase. Living light was chemistry.
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Glowing wood was burning with a slow fire, or giving back stored sunlight. Boyle showed the glow needed air but gave no heat, and Dubois showed it came from two chemicals that make light together with oxygen.
